1.0: The epigram is not here translated.
1.10: Poem 10, in which the poet complains that his mistress has asked him for money, is not here translated.
1.15: Poem 15, in which the poet boasts his work will outlive him, is not here translated.

1.1.1: For mighty wars I thought to tune my lute,
1.1.2: And make my measures to my subject suit.
1.1.3: Six feet for ev'ry verse the muse design'd,
1.1.4: But Cupid laughing, when he saw my mind,
1.1.5: From ev'ry second verse a foot purloin'd.
1.1.6: "Who gave thee, boy, this arbitrary sway,
1.1.7: On subjects, not thy own, commands to lay,
1.1.8: Who Phoebus only, and his laws obey?
1.1.9: 'Tis more absurd, than if the queen of love
1.1.10: Should in Minerva's arms to battle move;
1.1.11: Or manly Pallas from that queen should take
1.1.12: Her torch, and o'er the dying lover shake.
1.1.13: In fields as well may Cynthia sow the corn,
1.1.14: Or Ceres wind in woods the bugle-horn;
1.1.15: As well may Phoebus quit the trembling string,
1.1.16: For sword and shield; and Mars may learn to sing.
1.1.17: Already thy dominions are too large;
1.1.18: Be not ambitious of a foreign charge.
1.1.19: If thou wilt reign o'er all, and ev'ry where,
1.1.20: The god of music for his harp may fear.
1.1.21: Thus when with soaring wings I seek renown,
1.1.22: Thou pluck'st my pinions, and I flutter down.
1.1.23: Could I on such mean thoughts my muse employ,
1.1.24: I want a mistress, or a blooming boy."
1.1.25: Thus I complain'd; his bow the stripling bent,
1.1.26: And chose an arrow fit for his intent.
1.1.27: The shaft his purpose fatally pursues;
1.1.28: " Now, poet, there's a subject for thy muse,"
1.1.29: He said: (too well, alas, he knows his trade,)
1.1.30: For in my breast a mortal wound he made.
1.1.31: Far hence ye proud Hexameters remove,
1.1.32: My verse is pac'd, and tramell'd into love.
1.1.33: With myrtle wreaths my thoughtful brows enclose,
1.1.34: While in unequal verse I sing my woes.

1.2.1: Ah me! why am I so uneasy grown?
1.2.2: Ah! why so restless on my bed of down?
1.2.3: Why do I wish to sleep, but wish in vain?
1.2.4: Why am I all the tedious night in pain?
1.2.5: What cause is this, that ease, that rest denies?
1.2.6: And why my words break forth in gentle sighs?
1.2.7: Sure I should know if love had fix'd his dart;
1.2.8: Or creeps he softly in with treacherous art,
1.2.9: And then grows tyrant, there and wounds the heart?
1.2.10: 'Tis so, the shaft sticks deep, and galls my breast;
1.2.11: 'Tis tyrant love, that robs my thoughts of rest!
1.2.12: Well, shall I tamely yield, or must I fight?
1.2.13: I'll yield; 'tis patience makes a burden light:
1.2.14: A shaken torch grows fierce, and sparks arise;
1.2.15: But, if unmov'd, the fire looks pale and dies.
1.2.16: The hard-mouth'd horse smarts for his fierce disdain
1.2.17: The gentle's ridden with a looser rein.
1.2.18: Love smooths the gentle, but the fierce reclaims;
1.2.19: He fires their breasts, and fills their souls with flames.
1.2.20: I yield; great Love, my former crimes forgive,
1.2.21: Forget my rebel thoughts, and let me live;
1.2.22: No need of force: I willingly obey,
1.2.23: And now unarm'd, shall prove no glorious prey.
1.2.24: Go take thy mother's doves, thy myrtle crown,
1.2.25: And for thy chariot, Mars shall lend his own;
1.2.26: There thou shalt sit in thy triumphant pride,
1.2.27: And, whilst glad shouts resound on ev'ry side,
1.2.28: Thy gentle hands thy mother's doves shall guide.
1.2.29: And there to make thy glorious pomp and state,
1.2.30: A train of sighing youths, and maids shall wait,
1.2.31: Yet none complain of an unhappy fate.
1.2.32: There newly conquer'd I, still fresh my wound,
1.2.33: Will march along, my hands with myrtle bound;
1.2.34: There modesty, with veils thrown o'er her face,
1.2.35: Now doubly blushing at her own disgrace;
1.2.36: There sober thoughts, and whatso'er disdains
1.2.37: Love's rules, shall feel his power, and bear his chains:
1.2.38: Then all shall fear, all bow, yet all rejoice;
1.2.40: Thy constant guards, soft fancy, hope and fear,
1.2.41: Anger, and soft caresses shall be there:
1.2.42: By these strong guards are men and gods o'erthrown;
1.2.43: These conquer for thee, Love, and these alone,
1.2.44: Thy mother, from the sky thy pomp shall grace,
1.2.45: And scatter sweetest roses in thy face:
1.2.46: There glorious Love shall ride, profusely dress'd
1.2.47: With all the richest jewels of the east:
1.2.48: Rich gems thy quiver, and thy wheels infold,
1.2.49: And hide the poorness of the baser gold.
1.2.50: Then thou shalt conquer many, then.thy darts
1.2.51: Shall scatter thousand wounds on tender hearts:
1.2.52: Thy shafts themselves will fly, thy neighb'ring fire
1.2.53: Will catch mens' breasts, and kindle warm desire.
1.2.54: Thus conqu'ring Bacchus looks in Indian groves,
1.2.55: He drawn by tigers, thou by murm'ring doves.
1.2.56: Well then, since I too can increase thy train,
1.2.57: Spend not thy force on me, and rage in vain;
1.2.58: Look on thy kinsman Caesar's happy slaves,
1.2.59: The same victorious arm that conquers, saves.

1.3.1: Be just, dear maid, an equal passion prove,
1.3.2: Or show me cause why I should ever love.
1.3.3: I do not at your cold disdain repine,
1.3.4: Nor ask your love, do you but suffer mine.
1.3.5: I dare not aim at more exalted bliss,
1.3.6: And Venus will bestow her vot'ry this.
1.3.7: Take hin, who will for endless ages serve:
1.3.8: Take him whose faithful flame will never swerve
1.3.9: Though no illustrious names my race adorn;
1.3.10: Who am but of equestrian order born;
1.3.11: Though a few ploughs serve my paternal fields,
1.3.12: Nor my small table many dishes yields;
1.3.13: Yet Bacchus, Phoebus, and the tuneful nine,
1.3.14: Are all my friends, and to my side incline,
1.3.15: And love's great god, at last, will make me thine.
1.3.16: Heav'n knows, dear maid, I love no other fair;
1.3.17: In thee lives all my love, my heav'n lies there.
1.3.18: Oh! may I by indulgent Fate's decree,
1.3.19: With thee lead all my life, and die with thee.
1.3.20: Thy beauties yield me my transporting theme;
1.3.21: And while I celebrate thy charming name,
1.3.22: My verse shall be as sacred as my flame.
1.3.23: Jove's sev'ral rapes, his injur'd Io's wrongs,
1.3.24: Are made immortal in his poet's songs.
1.3.25: Verse still reveals where Leda's flames began,
1.3.26: Rais'd by the secret godhead in the swan,
1.3.27: The story of the rape Europa bore,
1.3.28: Shall last while winds shall rage, or waters roar.
1.3.29: Your name shall live like theirs, while verse endures,
1.3.30: And mine be ever writ, and read with yours.

1.4.1:
Dryden.
Your husband will be with us at the treat,
1.4.2: May that be the last supper he shall eat.
1.4.3: And am poor I, a guest invited there,
1.4.4: Only to see, while he may touch the fair?
1.4.5: To see you kiss, and hug your nauseous lord,
1.4.6: While his lewd hand descends below the board?
1.4.8: At such a sight, the Centaurs urg'd to arms:
1.4.9: That in a rage, they threw their cups aside,
1.4.10: Assail'd the bridegroom, and would force the bride.
1.4.11: I am not half a horse, (I would I were:)
1.4.12: Yet hardly can from you my hands forbear.
1.4.13: Take, then, my counsel; which observ'd, may be,
1.4.14: Of some importance both to you and me.
1.4.15: Be sure to come before your man be there,
1.4.16: There's nothing can be done, but come howe'er.
1.4.17: Sit next him, (that belongs to decency;)
1.4.18: But tread upon my foot in passing by.
1.4.19: Read in my looks what silently they speak,
1.4.20: And slily, with your eyes, your answer make.
1.4.21: My lifted eye-brow shall declare my pain,
1.4.22: My right hand to his fellow shall complain;
1.4.23: And on the back a letter shall design,
1.4.24: Beside a note that shall be writ in wine.
1.4.25: Whene'er you think upon our last embrace,
1.4.26: With your fore-finger gently touch your face.
1.4.27: If any word of mine offend my dear,
1.4.28: Pull with your hand the velvet of your ear;
1.4.29: If you are pleas'd with what I do or say,
1.4.30: Handle your rings, or vith your fingers play.
1.4.31: As suppliants use at altars, hold the board,
1.4.32: Whene'er you wish the devil may take your lord.
1.4.33: When he fills for you, never touch the cup,
1.4.34: But bid th' officious cuckold drink it up:
1.4.35: The waiter on those services employ;
1.4.36: Drink you, and I will snatch it from the boy,
1.4.37: Watching the part where your sweet mouth hath been,
1.4.38: And thence, with eager lips, will suck it in.
1.4.39: If he, with clownish manners, thinks it fit
1.4.40: To taste, and offer you the nasty bit,
1.4.41: Reject his greasy kindness, and restore
1.4.42: Th' unsav'ry morsel he had chew'd before.
1.4.43: Nor let his arms embrace your neck, nor rest
1.4.44: Your tender cheek upon his hairy breast;
1.4.45: Let not his hand within your bosom stray,
1.4.46: And rudely with your pretty bubbies play.
1.4.47: But, above all, let him no kiss receive,
1.4.48: That's an offence I never can forgive;
1.4.49: Do not, oh! do not that sweet mouth resign,
1.4.50: Lest I rise up in arms, and cry 'tis mine.
1.4.51: I shall thrust in betwixt, and void of fear
1.4.53: These things are plain to sight, but more I doubt
1.4.54: What you conceal beneath your petticoat;
1.4.55: Take not his leg between your tender thighs,
1.4.56: Nor with your hand provoke my foe to rise.
1.4.57: How many love inventions I deplore,
1.4.58: Which I myself have practis'd all before!
1.4.59: How oft have I been forc'd the robe to lift
1.4.60: In company; to make a homely shift
1.4.61: For a bare bout, ill huddled o'er in haste,
1.4.62: While o'er my side the fair her mantle cast!
1.4.63: You to your husband shall not be so kind,
1.4.64: But lest you should, your mantle leave behind.
1.4.65: Encourage him to tope, but kiss him not,
1.4.66: Nor mix one drop of water in his pot.
1.4.67: If he be fuddled well, and snores apace,
1.4.68: Then we may take advice from time and place.
1.4.69: When all depart, while compliments are loud,
1.4.70: Be sure to mix among the thickest crowd;
1.4.71: There I will be, and there we cannot miss,
1.4.72: Perhaps to grubble, or at least to kiss.
1.4.73: Alas, what length of labor I employ,
1.4.74: Just to secure a short and transient joy!
1.4.75: For night must part us, and when night is come
1.4.76: Tuck'd underneath his arm, he leads you home.
1.4.77: He locks you in, I follow to the door,
1.4.78: His fortune envy, and my own deplore;
1.4.79: He kisses you, he more than kisses too,
1.4.80: Th' outrageous cuckold thinks it all his due.
1.4.81: But add not to his joy by your consent,
1.4.82: And let it not be given, but only lent;
1.4.83: Return no kiss, nor move in any sort,
1.4.84: Make it a dull and a malignant sport.
1.4.85: Had I my wish he should no pleasure take,
1.4.86: But slubber o'er your bus'ness for my sake;
1.4.87: And whate'er fortune shall this night befall,
1.4.88: Coax me to morrow by forswearing all.

1.5.1: 'Twas noon when I, scorch'd with the double fire
1.5.2: Of the hot sun and my more hot desire,
1.5.3: Stretch'd on my downy couch at ease was laid,
1.5.4: Big with expectance of the lovely maid.
1.5.5: The curtains but half drawn, a light let in
1.5.6: Such as in shades of thickest groves is seen,
1.5.7: Such as remains when the sun flies away,
1.5.8: Or when night's gone, and yet it is not day.
1.5.9: This light to modest maids must be allow'd,
1.5.10: Where shame may hope its guilty head to shroud.
1.5.11: And now my love Corinna did appear,
1.5.12: Loose on her neck fell her divided hair;
1.5.13: Loose as her flowing gown, that wanton'd in the air.
1.5.14: In such a garb, with such a grace and mien,
1.5.15: To her rich bed came the Assyrian queen;
1.5.16: So Lais looked when all the youth of Greece
1.5.17: With adoration did her charms confess.
1.5.18: Her envious gown to pull away I tried,
1.5.19: But she resisted still, and still denied;
1.5.20: But so resisted that she seem'd to be
1.5.22: So I at last an easy conquest had,
1.5.23: Whilst my fair combatant herself betray'd.
1.5.24: But when she naked stood before my eyes,
1.5.25: Gods, with what charms did she my soul surprise!
1.5.26: What snowy arms did I both see and feel!
1.5.27: With what rich globes did her soft bosom swell!
1.5.28: Plump as ripe clusters rose each glowing breast,
1.5.29: Courting the hand, and suing to be press'd!
1.5.30: What a smooth plain was on her belly spread,
1.5.31: Where thousand little loves and graces play'd!
1.5.32: What thighs! what legs! but why strive I in vain,
1.5.33: Each limb, each grace, each feature to explain
1.5.34: One beauty did through her whole body shine;
1.5.35: I saw, admir'd, and press'd it close to mine
1.5.36: The rest who knows not? Thus entranc'd we lay,
1.5.37: Till in each other's arms we died away;
1.5.38: 0 give me such a noon, ye gods, to ev'ry day!

1.6.1: Slave, if thou worthy of thy chains wouldst be,
1.6.2: A grateful office do to love and me.
1.6.3: Unbar the wicket, and a friend admit;
1.6.4: The trouble is not much, nor favour great.
1.6.5: I ask thee not to spread the foldings wide;
1.6.6: Keep it at jar,-I'll softly by thee slide.
1.6.7: I to love's labours have so long been us'd,
1.6.8: My shapes are to a lath's lank size reduc'd.
1.6.9: The smallest crevice will my bus'ness do,
1.6.10: It cannot be so straight but I'll slip through.
1.6.11: Love guides me when by night I walk the street,
1.6.12: And when I grope my way directs my feet.
1.6.13: By night I was a youth afraid to walk,
1.6.14: Frighted by children and old nurses' talk;
1.6.15: I wonder'd men could wander in the gloom,
1.6.16: And kept, for fear of spirits, close at home.
1.6.17: Love and his mother, when they knew my care,
1.6.18: Cried, "Fool, thou shalt not long these phantoms fear."
1.6.19: Nor fear'd I long, for love my heart possess'd;
1.6.20: Those visions vanish'd, and my terrors ceas'd:
1.6.21: Nor ghosts nor scourers did I dread, but stroll'd
1.6.22: The streets a-nights, and grew in peril bold.
1.6.23: Thee only do I fear, and trembling stand
1.6.24: To wait the motions of thy tardy hand:
1.6.25: With soft request thy succour I implore,
1.6.26: Nor sue to Jove nor dread the Thund'rer more.
1.6.27: See how the gate is moistened with my tears!
1.6.28: What marks of my impatient love it bears!
1.6.29: Remember, when thou for the lash wert stripp'd
1.6.30: Who sav'd thee, at whose suit thou wert not whipp'd.
1.6.31: Did not I sooth thy angry lady's mind,
1.6.32: And make thy peace? Be thou to me as kind.
1.6.33: Think what soft things to move her soul I said,
1.6.34: And let them in a lover's favour plead.
1.6.35: But ah! the tender things that made her kind,
1.6.36: Work no such wonders on thy cruel mind.
1.6.37: Wouldst thou my friendly offices repay,
1.6.38: Fate throws a fair occasion in thy way;
1.6.39: Unlock the gate, the morning will not stay.
1.6.40: Unlock the gate; and as thou'rt kind to me,
1.6.41: So may thy gentle lady prove to thee;
1.6.42: May she to loose thy hateful chains incline,
1.6.43: And stead of water, be thy portion wine.
1.6.44: But what avail my soothing words? Thy ear
1.6.45: Is deaf, inhuman! to my moving pray'r.
1.6.46: Your gates with posts of pond'rous oak are barr'd,
1.6.47: As if your house was for a siege prepar'd;
1.6.48: Why all this fence? what foe have you to fear?
1.6.49: And why in peace do you provide for war?
1.6.50: Thus rudely if your lady's friends you treat,
1.6.51: What usage must her foes expect to meet?
1.6.52: Unlock the gate,-the morning will not stay;
1.6.53: Unlock the gate, and give my love its way.
1.6.54: Or is it sloth or is it sleep that brings,
1.6.55: This let to love, and pinions down his wings!
1.6.56: Why else do I in vain repeat my prayer,
1.6.57: Is it, thou dost not, or thou wilt not hear?
1.6.58: When first I waited at thy gate, and thought
1.6.59: To 'scape thy care, I was at midnight caught.
1.6.60: With over-dilligence thou then look'st out,
1.6.61: To spy what lover was upon the scout.
1.6.62: These are wild guesses, thou'rt perhaps employ'd
1.6.63: More sweetly, and enjoy'st what I enjoy'd.
1.6.64: And while I'm waiting with impatience here,
1.6.65: Thy envied fortune's with the faithless fair.
1.6.66: Oh, for thy pleasure, give me all thy pains,
1.6.67: Let us change chances, and be mine thy chains.
1.6.68: Unlock the gate, the morning will not stay,
1.6.69: Unlock the gate, and kindness past repay.
1.6.70: Hark: or I dream, or on the hinge I hear
1.6.71: The wicket turn, or bolts unloosen'd jar.
1.6.72: I dream, indeed, the bolts as they were laid,
1.6.73: Stand fix'd: the noise was by my fancy made.
1.6.74: But all, alas! is hush'd, I hear no sound,
1.6.75: All in the silence of the night is drown'd.
1.6.76: Here, hopeless of admittance, I attend,
1.6.77: While on my head the pearly dews descend.
1.6.78: Unlock the gate, the morning will not stay,
1.6.79: Unlock the gate, I will no longer pray,
1.6.80: But force by sword and fire my readier way.
1.6.81: What need of fire or sword? myself alone,
1.6.82: More pow'rful, than or sword or fire am grown.
1.6.83: Around your heads shall flaming torches fly,
1.6.84: And Jove the house shall burn, as well as I.
1.6.85: Night, love, and wine encourage and inflame:
1.6.86: These triumph over fear, and that o'er shame.
1.6.87: All ways I've tried, but all successless prove,
1.6.88: Nor threats can fright thee, nor entreaties move;
1.6.89: Deaf to my pray'rs as to my tears thou'rt blind,
1.6.90: Thy gate is less obdurate than thy mind.
1.6.91: But see, the ruddy morn begins to rise,
1.6.92: And paints with rosy streaks the eastern skies,
1.6.93: While crowing cocks the lab'rer's sloth revile,
1.6.94: And summon wretches to their daily toil.
1.6.95: Throw then, fond man, thy fragrant chaplet by,
1.6.96: And let it at thy lady's threshold lie.
1.6.97: When in the morn thy faded flow'rs she spies,
1.6.98: Kind thoughts of me may in her bosom rise,
1.6.99: Perhaps she may resent her porter's crime,
1.6.100: And grieve that here so ill I spent my time.
1.6.101: Against me though thou shut'st thy lady's gate,
1.6.102: I cannot one, that serves my mistress, hate.
1.6.103: You both who did against my hopes rebel,
1.6.104: Ah, porter; and ah, cruel gate, farewell.

1.7.1: Come, if ye're friends, and let these hands be bound,
1.7.2: Which could with impious rage a mistress wound:
1.7.3: What more did Ajax in his fury do,
1.7.4: When all the sacred grazing herd he slew?
1.7.5: Or he who spared not her who gave him breath?
1.7.6: So ill the son reveng'd his father's death!
1.7.7: Then I had broke the most religious ties,
1.7.8: Both to my parents and the deities:
1.7.9: I tore (0 heav'ns!) her finely braided hair,
1.7.10: How charming then look'd the disorder'd fair.
1.7.11: So Atalanta in her chaise is drawn,
1.7.12: Where the Arcadian beasts her empire own:
1.7.13: So Ariadne, left upon the shore,
1.7.14: Does all alone her lost estate deplore.
1.7.15: Who would not then have rail'd and talk'd aloud
1.7.16: (Which to the helpless sex might be allowed.)
1.7.17: She only did upbraid me with her eye,
1.7.18: Whose speaking tears did want of words supply.
1.7.20: Had struck me lame before that fatal hour,
1.7.21: And not have suffer'd me to pierce my heart
1.7.22: So deeply, in the best and tend'rest part;
1.7.23: To make a lady that subjection own,
1.7.24: Which is not to the meanest Roman known.
1.7.25: 'Twas Diomede, who first a goddess struck,
1.7.26: I from his hand that curs'd example took;
1.7.27: But he was far less criminal than I,
1.7.28: I was a lover, he an enemy.
1.7.29: March like a conqueror in triumph now,
1.7.30: With laurel wreaths encompassing your brow,
1.7.31: And render to the mighty gods your vow:
1.7.32: So, as you pass, th' attending gazing crowd,
1.7.33: By their applause shall speak your courage loud:
1.7.34: Let your sad captive in the front appear,
1.7.35: With streaming cheeks, and with dishevell'd hair.
1.7.36: Such lips were form'd for kinder words than these,
1.7.37: Wounds made by lovers' furious ecstasies.
1.7.38: Though like a torrent I was hurried on,
1.7.39: A slave to passion which I could not shun,
1.7.40: I might have only pierc'd her tender ear
1.7.41: With threatening language, such as virgins fear.
1.7.42: Fear having chill'd the current of her blood,
1.7.43: She pale as Parian marble statue stood;
1.7.44: Tears, which suspense did for a while restrain,
1.7.45: Gush'd forth, and down her cheeks the deluge ran.
1.7.46: As when the sun does by a powerful beam
1.7.47: Dissolve the frost, it runs into a stream.
1.7.48: The lamentable objects struck me dead,
1.7.49: And tears of blood to quench those tears I shed;
1.7.50: Thrice at her feet the prostrate suppliant fell,
1.7.51: And thrice did she repulse the criminal.
1.7.52: What would I not your anger to abate,
1.7.53: Redeem your favour, or remove your hate?
1.7.54: To your revenge no means or method spare;
1.7.55: Revenge, alas! is easy to the fair.

1.8.1: There is a bawd renown'd in Venus' wars,
1.8.2: Aud dreadful still with honorable scars;
1.8.3: Her youth and beauty, craft and guile supply,
1.8.4: Sworn foe to all degrees of chastity.
1.8.5: Dypsas, who first taught love-sick maids the way
1.8.6: To cheat the bridegroom on the wedding-day,
1.8.7: And then a hundred subtle tricks devis'd,
1.8.8: Wherewith the am'rous theft might be disguis'd;
1.8.9: Of herbs and spells she tries the guilty force,
1.8.10: The poison of a mare that goes to horse.
1.8.11: Cleaving the midnight air upon a switch,
1.8.12: Some for a bawd, most take her for a witch.
1.8.13: Each morning sees her reeling to her bed,
1.8.14: Her native blue o'ercome with drunken red:
1.8.15: Her ready tongue ne'er wants a useful lie,
1.8.16: Soft moving words, nor charming flattery.
1.8.17: Thus I o'erheard her to my Lucia speak:
1.8.18: "Young Damon's heart wilt thou for ever break
1.8.19: He long has lov'd thee, and by me he sends
1.8.20: To learn thy motions, which he still attends;
1.8.21: If to the park thou go'st, the plays are ill;
1.8.22: If to the plays, he thinks the air would kill.
1.8.23: The other day he gaz'd upon thy face,
1.8.24: As he would grow a statue in the place;
1.8.25: And who indeed does not? like a new star,
1.8.26: Beauty like thine strikes wonder from afar.
1.8.27: Alas! methinks thou art ill-dress'd to-night;
1.8.28: This point's too poor; thy necklace is not right;
1.8.29: This gown was by some botching tailor made,
1.8.30: It spoils thy shape; this fucus is ill laid.
1.8.31: Hear me, and be as happy as thou'rt fair:
1.8.32: Damon is rich, and what thou wanst, can spare.
1.8.33: Like thine his face, like thine his eyes are thought.
1.8.34: Would he not buy, he might himself be bought."
1.8.35: Fair Lucia blush'd. "It is a sign of grace,
1.8.36: (Dypsas replied,) that red becomes thy face.
1.8.37: All lovers now by what they give are weighed,
1.8.38: And she is best belov'd that best is paid;
1.8.39: The sun-burnt Latins, in old Tatius' reign,
1.8.40: Did to one man perhaps their love restrain:
1.8.41: Venus in her Aeneas' city rules,
1.8.42: And all adore her deity but fools.
1.8.43: Go on, ye fair, chaste only let such live
1.8.44: As none will ask, and know not how to give.
1.8.45: Life steals away, and our best hours are gone
1.8.46: Ere the true use or worth of them be known.
1.8.47: Things long neglected, of themselves decay;
1.8.48: What we forbear, time rudely makes his prey.
1.8.49: Beauty is best preserv'd by exercise,
1.8.50: Nor for that task can one or few suffice.
1.8.51: Wouldst thou grow rich, thou must from many take:
1.8.52: From one 'twere hard continually to rake.
1.8.53: Without new gowns and coaches, who can live?
1.8.54: What does thy poet but new verses give?
1.8.55: A poet, the last thing that earth does breed,
1.8.56: Whose wit, for sixpence, any one may read.
1.8.57: Hang the poor lover, and his pedigree;
1.8.58: The thriving merchant, or fat judge, give me.
1.8.59: Love truly none, but seem in love with all,
1.8.60: And at old friends to thy new lovers rail.
1.8.62: The sharp-set hawks will stoop to any lure.
1.8.63: Then grant again, lest he a habit get
1.8.64: Of living from thee; but be sure thou let
1.8.65: No empty lover in; murmur sometimes,
1.8.66: And at first hurt, reproach him with thy crimes.
1.8.67: Seem jealous, when thou'st been thyself to blame;
1.8.68: 'Twill stop his mouth, if thou the first complain.
1.8.69: All thou hast done be ready to forswear:
1.8.70: For lovers' oaths fair Venus has no ear.
1.8.71: Whilst lie is with thee, let some woman bring
1.8.72: Some Indian stuff or foreign precious thing;
1.8.73: Which thou must say thou want'st, and he must buy,
1.8.74: Though for it six months hence in gaol he lie.
1.8.75: Thy mother, sister, brother, and thy nurse,
1.8.76: Must have a pull each at thy lover's purse.
1.8.77: Let him from rivals never be secure,
1.8.78: That hope once gone, love will not long endure;
1.8.79: Show him the presents by those rivals sent,
1.8.80: So shall his bounty thy request prevent.
1.8.81: When he will give no more, ask him to lend:
1.8.82: If he wants money, find a trusting friend.
1.8.84: Or any thing for which his word will pass.
1.8.85: Practise these rules, thou'lt find the benefit!
1.8.86: I lost my beauty ere I got this wit."
1.8.87: I at that word step'd from behind the door,
1.8.88: And scarce my nails from her thin cheeks forbore.
1.8.89: Her few gray hairs in rage I vow'd to pull,
1.8.90: And thrust her drunken eyes into her skull.
1.8.91: "Poor in a dungeon's bottom may'st thou rot,
1.8.92: Die with a blow with thy beloved pot;
1.8.93: No brandy, and eternal thirst, thy lot."

1.9.1: Trust me, my Atticus, in love are wars;
1.9.2: And Cupid has his camp, as well as Mars:
1.9.3: The age that's fit for war best suits with love,
1.9.4: The old in both unserviceable prove,
1.9.5: Infirm in war, and impotent in love.
1.9.6: The soldiers which a general does require,
1.9.7: Are such as ladies would in bed desire:
1.9.8: Who but a soldier, and a lover, can
1.9.9: Bear the night's cold, in show'rs of hail and rain?
1.9.10: One in continual watch his station keeps,
1.9.11: Or on the earth in broken slumbers sleeps;
1.9.12: The other takes his still repeated round
1.9.13: By mistress' house — then lodges on the ground.
1.9.14: Soldiers, and lovers, with a careful eye,
1.9.15: Observe the motions of the enemy:
1.9.16: One to the walls makes his approach in form,
1.9.17: Pushes the siege, and takes the town by storm:
1.9.18: The other lays his close to Celia's fort,
1.9.19: Presses his point, and gains the wish'd-for port.
1.9.20: As soldiers, when the foe securely lies
1.9.21: In sleep, and wine dissolv'd, the camp surprise;
1.9.22: So when the jealous to their rest remove,
1.9.23: And all is hush'd, — the other steals to love.
1.9.24: You then, who think that love's an idle fit,
1.9.25: Know, that it is the exercise of wit.
1.9.26: In flames of love the fierce Achilles burns,
1.9.27: And, quitting arms, absent Briseis mourns:
1.9.29: Went Hector arm'd for war, and victory.
1.9.31: With hair dishevell'd, and disorder'd dress,
1.9.32: H' admir'd the beauties of the prophetess:
1.9.33: The god of war was caught in th' act of love;
1.9.34: A story know to all the court above.
1.9.35: Once did I pass my hours in sloth and ease,
1.9.36: Cool shades and beds of down could only please;
1.9.37: When a commanding beauty rais'd my mind,
1.9.38: I left all little trifling thoughts behind,
1.9.39: And to her service all my heart resign'd:
1.9.40: Since, like an active soldier, have I spent
1.9.41: My time in toils of war, in beauty's tent:
1.9.42: And for so sweet a pay all dangers underwent.
1.9.43: You see, my Atticus, by what I prove,
1.9.44: Who would not live in idleness-must love.

1.11.1: Nape, who know'st so well to set the hair,
1.11.2: And all the fashions of the modish fair,
1.11.3: Like thee no lady's woman in the town
1.11.4: Can forward an intrigue, or pin a gown;
1.11.5: No maid than thee can boast a quicker eye,
1.11.6: Nor sooner the sour husband's coming spy.
1.11.7: Here, Nape, take this billet-doux, and bear
1.11.8: My soul's soft wishes to the absent fair.
1.11.9: If I can guess, thy heart is not of flint,
1.11.10: Nor is there the least vein of iron in't;
1.11.11: I something in thy looks and manners see
1.11.12: Above the rudeness of thy low degree;
1.11.13: A softer turn, to pity more inclined,
1.11.14: Than vulgar souls, a more complacent mind;
1.11.15: Thou feel'st, if I can guess, an equal flame,
1.11.16: And thine and my distemper is the same.
1.11.17: If how I do, she asks, do thou reply,
1.11.18: For the dear night, and night's dear joys, I die.
1.11.19: Tell her the letter will the rest explain,
1.11.20: And does my soul, and all its hopes contain.
1.11.21: But time, while I am speaking, flies: be sure
1.11.22: To give the billet in a leisure hour:
1.11.23: Don't be content with her imperfect view,
1.11.24: But make her, when she has it, read it through.
1.11.25: I charge thee, as she reads, observe her eyes,
1.11.26: Catch, if thou canst, her gentle looks and sighs;
1.11.27: As these are sure presages of my joy,
1.11.28: So frowns and low'rs my flattering hopes destroy.
1.11.29: Pray her, when she has read it, to indite
1.11.30: An answer, and a long epistle write.
1.11.31: I hate a billet, where at once I view
1.11.32: A page all empty, but a line or two.
1.11.33: Let her without a margin fill it up,
1.11.34: And crowd it from the bottom to the top.
1.11.35: But why should I her pretty fingers tire?
1.11.36: A word's enough, and all that I desire.
1.11.37: Ah, Nape, let her only bid me come;
1.11.38: The page is large, which for that word has room.
1.11.39: Her letter, like a conqu'ror's, shall be bound
1.11.40: With bays, for it with conquests shall be crown'd.

1.12.1: Ah, pity me, my friends! the cruel fair
1.12.2: Will neither read my just complaint, nor hear.
1.12.3: The billet-doux I sent her she return'd,
1.12.4: And e'en to ope the tender letter scorn'd
1.12.5: Ill was the omen, for the slave I sent
1.12.6: Trip'd at the sill as out of doors he went.
1.12.7: If e'er you on an errand go for me,
1.12.8: More careful, sirrah! how you stumble, be;
1.12.10: The end's ne'er right if the beginning's wrong.
1.12.11: Sinee thus in vain her pity I implore,
1.12.12: I'll ne'er to tablets trust my passion more;
1.12.13: Nor with my wax for death my warrant seal;
1.12.14: Worse than her scorn, what torture can I feel?
1.12.15: From combs of Cosica the wax was ta'en,
1.12.16: The latent poison was the lover's bane.
1.12.17: Bees there from venom'd flow'rs their honey suck,
1.12.18: And surely to my wax that venom stuck.
1.12.19: Chance on the seal did my misfortune paint,
1.12.20: And show'd my doom by the vermilion teint.
1.12.21: Curse on the instruments of my disgrace!
1.12.22: May you lie rotting in some filthy place;
1.12.23: By carts run o'er may you to bits be torn,
1.12.24: And your mishap revenge Corinna's scorn!
1.12.25: The man that first to smooth your surface toil'd,
1.12.26: The wooden work with hands impure defil'd;
1.12.27: Gibbets and racks should of the wood be made,
1.12.28: And the rough tools of all the murd'ring trade.
1.12.29: Bats roosted in its branches as it grew,
1.12.30: And birds of prey for shelter thither flew:
1.12.31: The vulture, and all kind of rav'nous fowl,
1.12.32: There hatch their young, and there the om'nous owl.
1.12.33: How mad to use such tablets must I be?
1.12.34: Curst and ill fated, as their parent tree!
1.12.35: Were these fit things soft sentiments to bear,
1.12.36: And to a lady tell a lover's care?
1.12.37: Lawyers, on you, might horrid jargon write,
1.12.38: With sound the ear, with sense the soul to flight.
1.12.39: Well might your plain the wicked writings bear
1.12.40: Where the rich miser robs the ruin'd heir.
1.12.41: When I first purchas'd you, I feared no less,
1.12.42: Your numbers even made me doubt success:
1.12.43: May you by worms be in old age devour'd,
1.12.44: And by all mortals as by me abhor'd.

1.13.1: Aurora, rising from old Tithon's bed,
1.13.2: Does o'er the eastern skies her roses spread:
1.13.3: Stay, beauteous morn, awhile thy chariot stay,
1.13.4: Awhile with lagging wheels retard the day.
1.13.5: So may young birds, as often as the spring
1.13.6: Renews the year, o'er Memnon's ashes sing.
1.13.7: Now I lie folded in Corinna's arms,
1.13.8: And all her soul is mine, and all her charms;
1.13.9: I now am to her panting bosom press'd,
1.13.10: And now, if ever lover was, am bless'd.
1.13.11: As yet sweet sleep sits heavy on our eyes,
1.13.12: And warbling birds forbid, as yet to rise.
1.13.13: Stay, beauteous morning, for to love-sick maids
1.13.14: And youths, how grateful are these dusky shades!
1.13.15: All stay, and do not, from the blushing east,
1.13.16: With dawning glories break our balmy rest.
1.13.17: When night's black mantle does those glories hide,
1.13.18: The pilot by the stars his ship can guide,
1.13.19: And in mid-sea a certain course pursue,
1.13.20: As safe as when he has the sun in view.
1.13.21: What pleasure in thy light should mortals take?
1.13.22: Thou dost the weary traveller awake;
1.13.23: Though to the down his heavy head reclines,
1.13.24: Up he must lift it for the morning shines.
1.13.25: The soldier braces on his brazen shield,
1.13.26: Quits his warm tent, and fits him for the field:
1.13.27: The lab'ring hind his harrow takes, and now
1.13.28: The peasant yokes his oxen to the plough:
1.13.29: The boy half wak'd, and rubbing still his eyes,
1.13.30: Is loth alike to go to school, or rise;
1.13.31: While o'er his task he does imperfect nod,
1.13.32: He fears the ferula, he dreads the rod.
1.13.33: The bridegroom, starting from his bride's embrace,
1.13.34: Runs to his lawyer to consult his case;
1.13.35: A word is wanting in the dower deed,
1.13.36: And what to save the portion must he plead?
1.13.37: Now hungry serjeants quit their tempting ease,
1.13.38: To haunt the crowded courts and pick up fees.
1.13.39: Thy rise brings labour to the female band,
1.13.40: And puts the spindle in the spinster's hand:
1.13.41: Light are these toils, and little is the pain
1.13.42: To rise to work, and rest at night again;
1.13.43: But who that e'er knew love's transporting joys,
1.13.44: Could from the arms of youth and beauty rise?
1.13.45: Oft have I wish'd that night would keep her ground,
1.13.46: And all her stars be at thy rising found;
1.13.47: Oft have I wish'd the winds would stop thy way,
1.13.48: Repel thy car, or clouds involve the day.
1.13.49: Dost thou in envy lash each lazy steed,
1.13.50: And whirl thy chariot with unwonted speed?
1.13.51: Black was thy son, and in his hue's express'd
1.13.52: The gloomy passions of his parent's breats;
1.13.53: He, born of Cephalus, his ravish'd sire,
1.13.54: Is a known proof of thy adult'rous fire.
1.13.55: Thou, by his colour, wouldst thy crime conceal;
1.13.56: Ah, that to Tithon I the tale could tell!
1.13.57: Search all the records of Heaven's lechers round,
1.13.58: A fouler story cannot there be found.
1.13.59: In Cephalus' embraces when you lay,
1.13.60: And oft by theft renew'd your wanton play;
1.13.61: When Tithon's impotence you made your sport,
1.13.62: Did you not think the joyous moments short?
1.13.63: Lock'd in his arms did you in transports lie,
1.13.64: Ah! would you not, like me, to Phoebus cry,
1.13.65: "Stop, stop thy rapid course? Am I to blame
1.13.66: That Tithon's old, and cannot feel thy flame?
1.13.67: See how the moon does her Endymion keep
1.13.68: In night conceal'd, and drown'd in dewy sleep.
1.13.69: As lovely is the moon, as fair as thou,
1.13.70: Who freely, where she loves, her favours does bestow.
1.13.71: Jove, when he rob'd Amphitryon of his joy,
1.13.72: Did two whole nights in am'rous thefts employ;
1.13.73: Unknown when in Alcmena's arms he lay,
1.13.74: The night he doubles and suspends the day."
1.13.75: The morning heard my railing, and for shame
1.13.76: Blush'd that by force she must disturb my flame;
1.13.77: Bright Phoebus rushing forth, the glorious day
1.13.78: Drove the dear shades, that hid our joys, away.

1.14.1: I us'd to warn you, not with so much care,
1.14.2: And waste of ointment, to adorn your hair:
1.14.3: That warning now is useless, you have none,
1.14.4: And with your hair that trouble too is gone.
1.14.5: Where are the silken tresses, which adown
1.14.6: Your shoulders hung? A web was never spun
1.14.7: So fine, but, ah! those flowing curls are gone.
1.14.8: Ah fatal art! ah fatal care, and pains!
1.14.9: That robb'd me of the dearest of my chains.
1.14.10: Nor of a black, nor of a golden hue
1.14.11: They were, but of a dye between the two.
1.14.12: How could you hurt, or poison with perfume,
1.14.13: Those curls that were so easy to the comb?
1.14.14: That to no pains expos'd you, when you set
1.14.15: Their shining tresses for young hearts a net?
1.14.16: That ne'er provok'd you with your maids to war,
1.14.17: For hurting you with your entangled hair?
1.14.18: You ne'er were urg'd to some indecent fray,
1.14.19: Nor in a fury snatch'd the comb away.
1.14.20: The teeth ne'er touch'd you, and her constant care,
1.14.21: Without ill arts, would have preserv'd your hair.
1.14.22: Behind your chair I oft have seen her stand,
1.14.23: And comb and curl it with a gentle hand:
1.14.24: Oft have I seen it on your shoulders play
1.14.25: Uncomb'd, as on your purple bed you lay.
1.14.26: Your artless tresses with more charms appear,
1.14.27: Than when adorn'd with all your cost and care.
1.14.28: When on the grass the Thracian nymphs recline,
1.14.29: Of Bacchus full, and weary of their wine,
1.14.30: Less lovely are their locks, than yours, less fair
1.14.31: The ringlets of their soft dishevell'd hair:
1.14.32: Softer was thine, like fleecy down it felt,
1.14.33: And to the finger did as freely yield,
1.14.34: How didst thou torture it, the curls to turn,
1.14.35: Now with hot irons at thy toilet burn?
1.14.36: This rack, with what obedience did it bear?
1.14.37: "Ah spare," I cried, "thy patient tresses spare!
1.14.38: To hurt them is a sin: this needless toil
1.14.39: Forbear, and do not, what adorns thee, spoil.
1.14.40: 'Tis now too late to give your labour o'er,
1.14.41: Those tortur'd ringlets are, alas! no more.
1.14.42: Ah, cease the cruel thought, and cease to pass
1.14.43: Such irksome minutes at your faithful glass!
1.14.44: In vain thou seek'st thy silken locks to find;
1.14.45: Banish the dear remembrance from thy mind.
1.14.46: No weeds destroy'd them with their pois'nous juice,
1.14.47: Nor canst thou witches' magic charms accuse,
1.14.48: Nor rival's rage, nor dire enchantment blame,
1.14.49: Nor envy's blasting tongue, nor fever's flame.
1.14.50: The mischief by thy own fair hands was wrought;
1.14.51: Nor dost thou suffer for another's fault.
1.14.52: How oft I bade thee, but in vain, beware
1.14.53: The venom'd essence, that destroy'd thy hair?
1.14.54: Now with new arts thou shalt thy pride amuse,
1.14.55: And curls, of German captives borrow'd, use.
1.14.56: Drusus to Rome their vanquish'd nation sends
1.14.57: And the fair slave to thee her tresses lends.
1.14.58: With alien locks thou wilt thy head adorn,
1.14.59: And conquests gain'd by foreign beauties scorn.
1.14.60: How wilt thou blush, with other charms to please,
1.14.61: And cry, "How fairer were my locks than these!"
1.14.62: By heav'ns, to heart she takes her head's disgrace,
1.14.63: She weeps, and covers with her hands her face.
1.14.64: She weeps, as in her lap her locks she views;
1.14.65: What woman would not weep, such locks to lose!
1.14.66: Ah, that they still did on her shoulders flow,
1.14.67: Ah, that they now, where once they grew, did grow!
1.14.68: Take courage, fair Corinna, never fear,
1.14.69: Thou shalt not long these borrow'd tresses wear:
1.14.70: Time for your beauty shall this loss repair
1.14.71: And you again shall charm with native hair.

2.1: Poem 1, in which the poet introduces his second book, is not here translated.
2.2: Poem 2, addressed to Bagoe, is not here translated.
2.11: Poem 11, in which the poet prays that his Mistress will be safe as she travels by sea, is not here translated.

2.3.1: How hard's my hap, to have my fair consign'd
2.3.2: To one, who is imperfect in his kind;
2.3.3: To one, who ne'er can have the pow'r to prove
2.3.4: As woman, or as man, the mutual joys of love!
2.3.5: Who practis'd first on boys the cutting steel,
2.3.6: Deserv'd himself the fatal wound to feel.
2.3.7: Couldst thou be capable of Cupid's fires,
2.3.8: Or the least sensible of love's desires,
2.3.9: Some pity thou wouldst have on me, and grant
2.3.10: Thy aid, for what thou canst not know I want.
2.3.11: Ill suits thee now, the warrior's lance to wield,
2.3.12: To mount the manag'd horse, or lift the brazen shield:
2.3.13: Arms are for men, and not for such as thee,
2.3.14: Who shouldst from ev'ry manly thought be free.
2.3.15: No banner shouldst thou, but thy lady's bear,
2.3.16: And have no other leader but the fair.
2.3.17: Much it behoves thee then to strive to gain
2.3.18: Her favour, and thou need'st not strive in vain.
2.3.19: Consult her pleasure, and her will obey,
2.3.20: To favour that's the sure, the ready way:
2.3.21: Without it, how unhappy wilt thou be!
2.3.22: Life is without it of no use to thee.
2.3.23: Thou'rt beautiful, and mayst thy prime enjoy,
2.3.24: And well thy beauty and thy youth employ.
2.3.25: Study to serve thy gentle mistress well,
2.3.26: And merit her good graces by thy zeal;
2.3.27: Watch as thou wilt, the trouble thou mayst spare,
2.3.28: She'll easily deceive thy utmost care.
2.3.29: When two fond lovers are agreed to meet,
2.3.30: Canst thou their well-concerted plot defeat?
2.3.31: The ways of kindness thou shouldst rather use;
2.3.32: By being civil thou wilt nothing lose;
2.3.33: And when an opportunity is fail,
2.3.34: For thy own sake be friendly to our pray'r.
2.3.35: A friend be to thy lady, not a guard,
2.3.36: And we, with bounteous hand, thy friendship will reward.

2.4.1: Vice by my verse I never will defend,
2.4.2: Nor by false arms to fence my own pretend.
2.4.3: Frankly my failings I with shame confess;
2.4.4: To hide my errors would not make them less.
2.4.5: My faults, whate'er I suffer by't, I own,
2.4.6: That others, if they please, those faults may shun
2.4.7: I hate myself, my follies, and would fain
2.4.8: Be, were it in my pow'r, another man.
2.4.9: How difficult it is, ye righteous Gods,
2.4.10: Against our wills to bear such heavy loads.
2.4.11: I have not strength to guard myself from ill,
2.4.12: And, as I wish, to rule my wicked will.
2.4.13: I'm hurry'd on, as by the boistrous sea
2.4.14: The driving bark is swiftly borne away.
2.4.15: No certain form inflames my am'rous breast,
2.4.16: All beauty is alike to me the best;
2.4.17: A hundred causes kindle my desires,
2.4.18: And love ne'er wants a torch to light my fires.
2.4.19: When on the earth the modest virgin looks,
2.4.20: That very modesty of hers provokes;
2.4.21: And if I chance to meet a forward fair,
2.4.22: I'm taken with her frank and easy air:
2.4.23: I figure to myself a thousand charms,
2.4.24: A thousand raptures in her wanton arms.
2.4.25: If, like the damsels of the Sabine race,
2.4.26: She's rude, I look upon it as grimace;
2.4.27: That sullen as she seems at first, 'tis art,
2.4.28: That I the more may prize the conquest or her heart.
2.4.29: New joys, if she's a wit, I hope to find;
2.4.30: And with her body, to possess her mind:
2.4.31: If foolish, I in that can see no harm,
2.4.32: And in her very folly find a charm.
2.4.33: I know a maid so very fond, and dull,
2.4.34: To me she thinks Callimachus a fool.
2.4.35: I soon am pleas'd with one that's pleas'd with me,
2.4.36: Alike we in our taste and wish agree:
2.4.37: But if the fair my verses don't approve,
2.4.38: I bragging tell her, she will like my love;
2.4.39: If with her tongue, or with her heel she's brisk,
2.4.40: Her prattle pleases, and her gamesome frisk;
2.4.41: But if she's heavy, I suppose at night
2.4.42: She'll change, and prove, as I would have her, light,
2.4.43: The fair that sings, enchants me with her voice;
2.4.44: Oh, what a gust it gives a lover's joys!
2.4.45: When her shrill shakes afresh his bosom wound,
2.4.46: And from her lips he kisses off the sound;
2.4.47: When her soft fingers touch the silver strings,
2.4.48: And sweetly to the sounding lute she sings;
2.4.49: Who can resist such strong redoubled charms?
2.4.50: Her music melts me, as her beauty warms
2.4.51: If in the dance the nimble nymph I find,
2.4.52: And view how she her pliant limbs does wind,
2.4.53: How artfully she to the music moves,
2.4.54: I cry, "How happy is the man she loves!"
2.4.55: My humour, in a word, is plainly this,
2.4.56: All objects please, and nothing comes amiss.
2.4.57: To love, and be belov'd my sole employ:
2.4.58: Dispos'd to be enjoy'd, and to enjoy.
2.4.59: This lady for her length I like, her spread
2.4.60: Will swell my arms, and fill the joyous bed;
2.4.61: She's like the lusty heroines of old,
2.4.62: And with a strong embrace her lover will enfold.
2.4.63: This lass, because she's little, I approve;
2.4.64: The least are lightest in the sports of love.
2.4.65: With every size my passion does agree,
2.4.66: And tall and short are both alike to me.
2.4.67: I fancy, when undress'd I find the fair,
2.4.68: 'Tis less her want of charms, than want of care.
2.4.69: If with her dishabille, I cry, " I'm pleas'd,"
2.4.70: How beauteous would she be if she were dress'd
2.4.71: And when she does her best apparel wear,
2.4.72: I think her riches in her pride appear.
2.4.73: The fair, the olive, are to me the same,
2.4.74: Alike the swarthy, and the sandy dame.
2.4.75: When her black curls adown her shoulders flow,
2.4.76: Such Leda's were, her skin as white as snow;
2.4.77: And when her golden locks her head adorn,
2.4.78: I straight compare her to the saffron morn.
2.4.79: My love with no complexion disagrees,
2.4.80: But all alike my ready passion please.
2.4.81: The younger by their bloom my heart secure,
2.4.82: The elder win it as they're more mature;
2.4.83: And though the younger may excel in charms,
2.4.84: The elder clasp you with experienc'd arms
2.4.85: What all the city like, is liked by me,
2.4.86: And I with them and all my loves agree.
2.4.87: I'm proud to be the rival of the town,
2.4.88: And to their taste will still conform my own.

2.5.1: Cupid, be gone! I can for beauty sigh,
2.5.2: But not be forc'd to wish each hour to die;
2.5.3: For so I wish whene'er my restless thoughts
2.5.4: Dwell on her falsehoods and repeated faults.
2.5.5: All other plagues know sometimes to be civil,
2.5.6: But woman is a sure, perpetual evil.
2.5.7: No pimp I bribe to prove thy perjur'd vows,
2.5.9: 0, cou dst thou but my arguments disprove!
2.5.10: A cause so good is here unwish'd in love.
2.5.11: Happy, who dares t' avow his censur'd flame,
2.5.12: And vindicate the secret tripping dame.
2.5.13: Blushless, tho' guilty, with uplifted eyes,
2.5.14: "'Tis false, my life, by yon bright Heaven," she cries.
2.5.15: Himself he fools, and madly feeds his grief,
2.5.16: Who from conviction seeks the sad relief.
2.5.17: Wretched I saw thy wantonness unsought,
2.5.18: By thee in sleep secure and eyeless thought;
2.5.19: With glances on each other how you hung!
2.5.20: How ev'ry nod had more than half a tongue!
2.5.21: How roll'd thy glowing eyes! how lewd they spoke!
2.5.22: E'en from thy artful fingers language broke;
2.5.23: While writing on the board with pens they vied,
2.5.24: And the spilt wine the want of ink supplied.
2.5.25: The silent speech too well I understood,
2.5.26: For to deceive a lover yet who could?
2.5.27: Tho' thou didst write in a laconic hand,
2.5.28: And words for sentences were taught to stand.
2.5.29: Now ended was the treat, and ev'ry guest
2.5.30: Indulg'd his ease, and lay compos'd to rest:
2.5.31: Your close, lascivious kisses then I spied,
2.5.32: And something more than lips to lips applied;
2.5.33: Such from a sister brothers ne'er receive,
2.5.34: But yielding fair ones to warm lovers give.
2.5.35: Not so Diana would to Phoebus press,
2.5.36: But Cytherea so her Mars would bless.
2.5.37: Too far provok'd, at last I cried aloud,
2.5.38: "On whom are pleasures, due to me, bestow'd?
2.5.39: I must not, will not, cannot bear this sight;
2.5.40: 'Tis lawful, sure, to seize upon my right.
2.5.41: These raptures to us both in common are,
2.5.42: But whence, ye furies, claims a third his share?"
2.5.43: Enrag'd I spoke, and o'er her cheeks were spread
2.5.44: Swift newborn glories in a sudden red;
2.5.45: Such blushes on the bridal night adorn
2.5.46: The trembling virgin; such the rising morn.
2.5.47: So sweet a hue the lab'ring Cynthia shows,
2.5.48: Or the fair lily damask'd by the rose;
2.5.49: Or iv'ry, which time's yellow taint defies,
2.5.50: When twice enrich'd with proud Assyrian dies:
2.5.51: Such were her looks, and a diviner grace
2.5.52: Had never brighten'd that enchanting face.
2.5.53: She cast her eyes down on the humble ground;
2.5.54: Her eyes, so cast, an unknown sweetness found.
2.5.55: Mournful her looks; her mournful looks became
2.5.56: Shining thro' grief, and beautiful in shame.
2.5.57: I rush'd, resolv'd her golden locks to tear,
2.5.58: And with mad violence disrobe the fair;
2.5.59: But as I viewed her face, th' extended hand
2.5.60: Shrunk back, nor hearken'd to the harsh command.
2.5.61: Others protection seek by dint of arms,
2.5.62: Her only safeguard was—her wondrous charms.
2.5.63: I, who but late look'd insolently brave,
2.5.64: Fell from my height, and couch'd a suppliant slave:
2.5.65: I rav'd no longer at another's bliss,
2.5.66: But begg'd the transport of as sweet a kiss.
2.5.67: Smiling she said, " How grateful thy request!
2.5.68: If e'er my kisses please thee, take the best."
2.5.69: Oh, with what gust as from her soul they came!
2.5.70: Such might melt Jove, and stop the vengeful flame;
2.5.71: I fear'd my rival too enjoy'd the same.
2.5.72: These, better than from me she learn'd I thought,
2.5.73: Something taught new, alas! I wish'd untaught;
2.5.74: What most gave pleasure, that now stings the most;
2.5.75: Why were our darting tongues entirely lost?
2.5.76: Nor fret I thou in kissing shouldst excel,
2.5.77: And yet 'tis strange to know to kiss so well;
2.5.78: But ah! such lectures only could be read
2.5.79: By youthful tutors, and imbib'd abed.
2.5.80: That sage who'er these large improvements made,
2.5.81: Was by his pupil preciously repay'd.

2.6.1:
Creech.
Alas! poor Poll, my Indian talker, dies!
2.6.2: Go, birds, and celebrate his obsequies;
2.6.3: Go, birds, and beat your breasts, your faces tear,
2.6.4: And pluck your gaudy plumes instead of hair;
2.6.5: Let doleful tunes the frighted forest wound,
2.6.6: And your sad notes supply the trumpet's sound.
2.6.7: Why, Philomel, dost mourn the Thracian rage?
2.6.8: It is enough, thy grief at last assuage;
2.6.9: His crimson faults are now grown white with age.
2.6.10: Now mourn this bird; the cause of all thy woe
2.6.11: Was great, 'tis true, but it was long ago.
2.6.12: Mourn, all ye wing'd inhabitants of air,
2.6.13: But you, my turtle, take the greatest share;
2.6.14: You too liv'd constant friends and free from strife
2.6.15: Your kindness was entire, and long as life:
2.6.16: What Pylades to his Orestes vow'd.
2.6.17: To thee, poor Poll, thy friendly turtle show'd,
2.6.18: And kept his love as long as fate allow'd.
2.6.19: But, ah! what did thy faith, thy plumes, and tail,
2.6.20: And what thy pretty speaking art, avail?
2.6.21: And what that thou wert giv'n, and pleas'd my miss,
2.6.22: Since now the bird's unhappy glory dies?
2.6.23: A lovely verdant green grac'd ev'ry quill,
2.6.24: The deepest vivid red did paint thy bill;
2.6.25: In speaking thou didst ev'ry bird excel,
2.6.26: None prattled, and none lisp'd the words so well.
2.6.27: 'Twas envy only sent this fierce disease;
2.6.28: Thou wert averse to war, and liv'dst in peace,
2.6.29: A talking harmless thing, and lov'dst thine ease.
2.6.30: The fighting quails still live 'midst all their strife,
2.6.31: And even that, perhaps, prolongs their life.
2.6.32: Thy meat was little, and thy prattling tongue
2.6.33: Would ne'er permit to make thy dinner long:
2.6.34: Plain fountain water all thy drink allow'd,
2.6.35: And nut and poppy-seed were all thy food.
2.6.36: The preying vultures and the kites remain,
2.6.37: And the unlucky crow still caws for rain;
2.6.38: The chough still lives 'midst fierce Minerva's hate,
2.6.39: And scarce nine hundred years conclude her fate;
2.6.40: But my poor Poll now hangs his sickly head,
2.6.41: My Poll, my present from the east, is dead.
2.6.42: Best things are sooner snatch'd by cov'tous fate,
2.6.43: To worse she freely gives a longer date;
2.6.45: And Hector fell, whilst all his brothers liv'd.
2.6.46: Why should I tell what vows Corinna made?
2.6.47: How oft she begg'd thy life, how oft she pray'd?
2.6.48: The seventh day came, and now the Fates begin
2.6.49: To end the thread, they had no more to spin;
2.6.50: Yet still he talk'd, and when death nearer drew,
2.6.51: His last breath said, "Corinna, now adieu!"
2.6.52: There is a shady cypress grove below,
2.6.53: And thither (if such doubtful things we know)
2.6.54: The ghosts of pious birds departed go;
2.6.55: 'Tis water'd well, and verdant all the year,
2.6.56: And birds obscene do never enter there;
2.6.57: There harmless swans securely take their rest,
2.6.58: And there the single Phoenix builds her nest;
2.6.59: Proud peacocks there display their gaudy train,
2.6.60: And billing turtles coo o'er all the plain:
2.6.61: To these dark shades my parrot's soul shall go,
2.6.62: And with his talk divert the birds below;
2.6.63: Whilst here his bones enjoy a noble grave,
2.6.64: A little marble, and an epitaph:-
2.6.65: "In talking I did ev'ry bird excel,
2.6.66: And my tomb proves my mistress lov'd me well."

2.7.1: And must I still be guilty, still untrue,
2.7.2: And when old crimes are purg'd, still charg'd with new?
2.7.3: What tho' at last my cause I clearly gain?
2.7.4: Yet I'm asham'd so oft to strive in vain,
2.7.5: And when the prize will scarce reward the pain.
2.7.6: If at the play I in fop-corner sit,
2.7.7: And with a squinting eye gloat o'er the pit,
2.7.8: Or view the boxes, you begin to fear,
2.7.9: And fancy straight some rival beauty there.
2.7.10: If any looks on me, you think you spy
2.7.11: A private assignation in her eye;
2.7.12: A silent soft discourse in ev'ry grace,
2.7.13: And tongues in all the features of her face.
2.7.14: If I praise any one, you tear your hair,
2.7.15: Show frantic tricks, and rage with wild despair;
2.7.17: I strive to cloak my passion by the cheat.
2.7.18: If I look well, I then neglect your charms,
2.7.19: Lie dull and lazy in your active arms;
2.7.20: If weak my voice, if pale my looks appear,
2.7.21: 0 then I languish for another fair.
2.7.22: Would I did sin, and you with cause complain,
2.7.23: For when we strive to shun, yet strive in vain,
2.7.24: 'Tis comfort sure to have deserv'd the pain.
2.7.25: But sure fond fancies now such heats engage,
2.7.26: Your cred'lous peevish humour spoils your rage.
2.7.27: In frequent chidings I no force can see,
2.7.28: You frown too often to prevail with me;
2.7.29: The ass grows dull by stripes; the constant blow
2.7.30: Beats off his briskness, and he moves but slow.
2.7.31: But now I'm lavish of my kind embrace,
2.7.32: And Moll, forsooth, supplies her lady's place!
2.7.33: Kind love, forbid that I should stoop so low;
2.7.34: What! unto mean, ignoble beauties bow?
2.7.35: A chambermaid! no faith, my love flies high;
2.7.36: My quarry is a miss of quality.
2.7.37: Fye, who would clasp a slave? who joy to feel
2.7.38: Her hands of iron and her sides of steel?
2.7.39: 'Twill damp an eager thought, 'twill check my mind,
2.7.40: To feel those knobs the lash hath left behind.
2.7.41: Besides, she dresses well, with lovely grace
2.7.42: She sets thy tow'r, and does adorn thy face;
2.7.43: Thy nat'ral beauty all her hearts improve,
2.7.44: And make me more enamour'd of my love.
2.7.45: Then why should I tempt her, and why betray
2.7.46: Thy useful slave, and have her turn'd away?
2.7.47: I swear by Venus, by love's darts and bow,
2.7.48: (A desp'rate oath, you must believe me now,)
2.7.49: I am not guilty, I've not broke my vow!

2.8.1: Dear, skilful Betty, who dost far excel
2.8.2: My lady's other maids in dressing well;
2.8.3: Dear Betty, fit to be preferred above
2.8.4: To Juno's chamber, or the queen of love;
2.8.6: Not easy to deny desired joy;
2.8.7: Thro' whose soft eyes still secret wishes shine,
2.8.8: Fit for thy mistress' use, but more for mine;
2.8.9: Who, Betty, did the fatal secret see?
2.8.10: Who told Corinna you were kind to me!
2.8.11: Yet when she chid me for my kind embrace,
2.8.12: Did any guilty blush spread o'er my face!
2.8.13: Did I betray thee, maid, or could she spy
2.8.14: The least confession in my conscious eye!
2.8.15: Not that I think it a disgrace to prove
2.8.16: Stol'n sweets, or make a chambermaid my love;
2.8.18: Atrides bow'd to fair Cassandra's charms:
2.8.19: Sure I am less than these,-then what can bring
2.8.20: Disgrace to me, that so became a king!
2.8.21: But when she look'd on you, poor harmless maid,
2.8.22: You blush'd, and all the kind intrigue betray'd;
2.8.23: Yet still I vow'd, I made a stout defence,
2.8.24: I swore, and look'd as bold as innocence;
2.8.26: Kind Venus, do not hear my perjury;
2.8.27: Kind Venus, stop thy ears when lovers lie.
2.8.28: Now, Betty, how will you my oaths requite?
2.8.29: Come, pr'ythee let's compound for more delight;
2.8.30: Faith, I am easy, and but ask a night.
2.8.31: What! start at the proposal? how! deny
2.8.32: Pretend fond fears of a discovery?
2.8.33: Refuse, lest some sad chance the thing betray?
2.8.34: Is this your kind, your damn'd obliging way?
2.8.35: Well, deny on; I'll lie, I'll swear no more;
2.8.36: Corinna now shall know thou art a whore.
2.8.37: I'll tell, since you my fair address forbid,
2.8.38: How often, when, and where, and what we did!

2.9.1:
Rochester.
O Love! how cold and slow to take my part,
2.9.2: Thou idle wanderer about my heart!
2.9.3: Why thy old faithful soldier wilt thou see
2.9.4: Oppress'd in thy own tents? they murder me;
2.9.5: Thy flames consume, thy arrows pierce thy friends;
2.9.6: Rather on foes pursue more noble ends.
2.9.8: A cure as certain as it gave the blow.
2.9.9: Hunters, who follow flying game, give o'er
2.9.10: When the prey's caught, hope still leads on before;
2.9.11: We, thine own slaves, feel thy tyrannic blows.
2.9.12: While thy tame hand's unmov'd against thy foes.
2.9.13: On men disarm'd, how can you gallant prove?
2.9.14: And I was long ago disarm'd by love.
2.9.15: Millions of dull men live, and scornful maids;
2.9.16: We'll own love valiant when he these invades.
2.9.17: Rome from each corner of the wide world snatch'd
2.9.18: A laurel, or't had been to this day thatch'd;
2.9.19: But the old soldier has his resting-place,
2.9.20: And the good batter'd horse is turn'd to grass:
2.9.21: The harass'd whore, who liv'd a wretch to please,
2.9.22: Has leave to be a bawd, and take her ease.
2.9.23: For me then, who have truly spent my blood,
2.9.24: Love, in thy service, and so boldly stood
2.9.25: In Celia's trenches, were't not wisely done,
2.9.26: E'en to retire, and live at peace at home?
2.9.27: No-might I gain a godhead to disclaim
2.9.28: My glorious title to my endless flame,
2.9.29: Divinity with scorn I would forswear,
2.9.30: Such sweet, dear, tempting devils women are.
2.9.31: Whene'er those flames grow faint, I quickly find
2.9.32: A fierce black storm pour down upon my mind;
2.9.33: Headlong I'm hurl'd like horsemen who in vain
2.9.35: As ships, just when the harbour they attain,
2.9.36: Are snatch'd by sudden blasts to sea again,
2.9.37: So Love's fantastic storms reduce my heart,
2.9.38: Half rescu'd, and the god resumes his dart.
2.9.39: Strike here, this undefended bosom wound,
2.9.40: And for so brave a conquest be renown'd.
2.9.41: Shafts fly so fast to me from ev'ry part,
2.9.42: You'll scarce discern the quiver from my heart.
2.9.43: What wretch can bear a livelong night's dull rest,
2.9.44: Or think himself in lazy slumbers blest?
2.9.45: Fool-is not sleep the image of pale death?
2.9.46: There's time for rest when fate has stopp'd your breath.
2.9.47: Me may my soft deluding dear deceive,
2.9.48: I'm happy in my hopes, while I believe:
2.9.49: Now let her flatter, then as fondly chide,
2.9.50: Often may I enjoy, oft be denied.
2.9.51: With doubtful steps the god of war does move,
2.9.52: By thy example, in ambiguous love.
2.9.53: Blown to and fro, like down from thy own wing,
2.9.54: Who knows when joy or anguish thou wilt bring?
2.9.55: Yet at thy mother's and thy slave's request,
2.9.56: Fix an eternal empire in my breast;
2.9.57: And let th' inconstant charming sex,
2.9.58: Whose wilful scorn does lovers vex,
2.9.59: Submit their hearts before thy throne;
2.9.60: The vassal world is then thy own.

2.10.1:
Ovid tells Graecinus, that he is fallen in love with a couple of ladies. By an unknown hand.
What you affirm'd, my friend, is prov'd untrue,
2.10.2: That none at once could madly dote on two.
2.10.3: Deceiv'd, unarm'd, we Cupid soon o'ercame,
2.10.4: And I glow shameless with a double flame.
2.10.5: They both are fair, both dress'd so nicely well,
2.10.6: That the pre-eminence is hard to tell.
2.10.7: Sometimes for this, sometimes for that I burn,
2.10.8: And each more beauteous sparkles in her turn.
2.10.9: Each claims my passion, and my heart divides
2.10.10: As to and fro the doubtful galliot rides.
2.10.11: Here driven by winds, and there redriven by tides.
2.10.12: Why doubly chain'd? was not a single fair
2.10.13: Enough to load me with perpetual care?
2.10.14: Why are more leaves brought to the shady wood,
2.10.15: Stars to the sky, or waters to the flood?
2.10.16: Yet better so than not to love at all;
2.10.17: Still on my foes may such dull blessings fall.
2.10.18: May they, insipidly supine, be spread
2.10.19: Along the middle of a widowed bed;
2.10.20: While I with sprightliness love's vigil's keep,
2.10.21: Stretch'd out for something far more sweet than sleep.
2.10.22: Others from ruin fly, to mine I run,
2.10.23: To be by women pleasingly undone,
2.10.24: Longing for two, since undestroy'd by one.
2.10.25: Still let my slender limbs for love suffice;
2.10.26: I want no nerves, but want the bulky size.
2.10.27: My limbs, tho' lean are not in vain display'd;
2.10.28: From me no female ever rose a maid.
2.10.29: Oft have I, when a luscious night was spent,
2.10.30: Saluted morn, nor cloy'd nor impotent.
2.10.31: Happy, who gasps in love his latest breath;
2.10.32: Give me, ye gods, so softly sweet a death!
2.10.33: Let the rough warriors grapple on the plain,
2.10.34: And with their blood immortal honour gain;
2.10.35: Let the vile miser plough for wealth the deep,
2.10.36: And, shipwrek'd in the unfatbom'd waters, sleep
2.10.37: May Venus grant me but my last desire,
2.10.38: In the full height of rapture to expire.
2.10.39: Perhaps some friend, with kindly dew supplied,
2.10.40: Weeping will say, "As Ovid liv'd, he died."

2.12.1: Io Triumphe! I have won the prize,
2.12.2: For in my arms the fair Corinna lies.
2.12.3: Nor jealous husband, nor a guardian's care,
2.12.4: Nor door defended with a double bar,
2.12.5: Could fence against a lover's artifice,
2.12.6: For in my arms the fair Corinna lies.
2.12.7: With reason of my victory I boast,
2.12.8: The conquest gain'd, and yet no blood is lost;
2.12.9: I scal'd no walls, I pass'd no ditch profound,
2.12.10: Safe were my wars, and all without a wound.
2.12.11: My only work a charming girl to gain;
2.12.12: The pleasure well rewards the little pain.
2.12.13: Ten years the Greeks did in one siege employ,
2.12.14: But levell'd were, at length, the walls of Troy;
2.12.15: What glory was there by th' Atrides won,
2.12.16: So many chiefs before a single town!
2.12.17: Not thus did I my pleasant toils pursue,
2.12.18: And the whole glory to myself is due;
2.12.19: Myself was horse and foot, myself alone
2.12.20: The captain and the soldier was in one,
2.12.21: And fought beneath no banner but my own.
2.12.22: Whether by strength I combated, or wile,
2.12.23: Fortune did ever on my actions smile;
2.12.24: I only owe my triumph to my care,
2.12.25: And by my patience only won the fair.
2.12.26: Nor was my cause of quarrel new; the same
2.12.27: Set Europe and proud Asia in a flame.
2.12.28: For Helen, ravish'd by the Dardan boy,
2.12.29: Was the war wag'd that sunk the pride of Troy;
2.12.30: The Centaurs double form'd, half man, half beast,
2.12.31: Defil'd with horrid war the nuptial feast;
2.12.32: Inflam'd by wine and woman's magic charms,
2.12.33: They turn'd the jolly face of joy to arms.
2.12.34: 'Twas woman urg'd the strife; a second fair
2.12.35: Involv'd the Trojans in a second war.
2.12.36: What wreck, what ruin, did a Woman bring
2.12.37: On peaceful Latium, and its pious king!
2.12.38: When Rome was young and in her infant state
2.12.39: What woes did woman to our sires create!
2.12.40: Into what peril was that city brought,
2.12.41: When Sabine fathers for their daughters fought!
2.12.42: Two lusty bulls I in the meads have view'd
2.12.43: In combat join'd, and by their side there stood
2.12.44: A milk-white heifer, who provok'd the fight,
2.12.45: By each contended, but the conqueror's right;
2.12.46: She gives them courage, her they both regard,
2.12.47: As one that caus'd the war, and must reward.
2.12.48: Compell'd by Cupid in his host to list
2.12.49: (And who that has a heart can love resist?)
2.12.50: His soldier I have been, without the guilt
2.12.51: Of blood, in any of our battles spilt;
2.12.52: For him I've fought, as many more have done,
2.12.53: And many rivals met, but murder'd none.

2.13.1:
Corinna, and prevent her miscarrying.
With cruel art Corinna would destroy
2.13.2: The ripening fruit of our repeated joy.
2.13.3: While on herself she practises her skill,
2.13.4: She's like the mother, not the child, to kill.
2.13.5: Me she would not acquaint with what she did,
2.13.6: From me a thing, which I abhorr'd, she hid;
2.13.7: Well might I now be angry, but I fear,
2.13.8: Ill as she is, I might endanger her.
2.13.9: By me, I must confess, she did conceive,
2.13.10: The fact is so, or else I so believe;
2.13.11: We've cause to think, what may so likely be,
2.13.12: So is, and then the babe belongs to me
2.13.13: Oh Isis, who delight'st to haunt the fields,
2.13.14: Where fruitful Nile his golden harvest yields,
2.13.15: Where with seven mouths into the sea it falls,
2.13.16: And hast thy walks around Canope's walls,
2.13.17: Who Memphis visit'st, and the Pharian tower,
2.13.18: Assist Corinna with thy friendly powers.
2.13.19: Thee by thy silver Sistra I conjure,
2.13.20: A life so precious by thy aid secure;
2.13.21: So mayst thou with Osiris still find grace:
2.13.23: I pray thee, so may still thy rights divine
2.13.24: Flourish, and serpents round thy offerings twine
2.13.25: May Apis with his horns the pomp attend,
2.13.26: And be to thee, as thou'rt to her, a friend.
2.13.27: Look down, oh Isis! on the teeming fair,
2.13.28: And make at once her life and mine thy care:
2.13.29: Have pity on her pains; the help you give
2.13.30: To her, her lover saves, in her I live.
2.13.31: From thee this favour she deserves; she pays
2.13.32: Her vows to thee on all thy solemn days;
2.13.33: And when the Galli at thy altars wait,
2.13.34: She's present at the feast they celebrate.
2.13.35: And thou, Lucina, who the labouring womb
2.13.36: Dost with compassion view, to her assistance come:
2.13.37: Nor dost thou, when to thee thy votaries pray
2.13.38: For speedy help, thy wanted help delay.
2.13.40: Thy votary she, and worthy of thy care.
2.13.41: I'll with my off'rings to thy altar come,
2.13.42: With votive myrrh thy sacred fane perfume;
2.13.43: The vows I make that thou my fair mayst bless,
2.13.44: In words inscrib'd, I'll on thy shrine express:-
2.13.46: The goddess here, the teeming dame to aid."
2.13.47: Ah, goddess! of my humble suit allow;
2.13.48: Give place to my inscription and my vow.
2.13.49: If frighted as I am, I may presume
2.13.50: Your conduct to direct in time to come,
2.13.51: Corinna, since you've suffer'd thus before,
2.13.52: Ah, try the bold experiment no more!

2.14.1: What boots it that the fair are free from war,
2.14.2: And what that they're forbid the shield to bear,
2.14.3: Against themselves if they knew arms employ
2.14.4: And madly with new wounds their lives destroy?
2.14.5: The cruel mother who did first contrive
2.14.6: Her babe to butcher ere 'twas scarce alive,
2.14.7: Who thus from nature's tender dictates swerv'd,
2.14.8: To perish by her proper hands deserv'd.
2.14.9: Why do the sex forget their softness? why
2.14.10: Such projects for a foolish fancy try?
2.14.11: The belly must be smooth, no wrinkle there
2.14.12: To shock the lover's wanton glance appear;
2.14.13: His touch as well as sight they fain would please,
2.14.14: And the womb early of its burden ease.
2.14.15: Had woman sooner known this wicked trade,
2.14.16: Among the race of men what havock had they made.
2.14.17: Mankind had been extinct, and lost the seed,
2.14.18: Without a wonder to restore the breed,
2.14.19: As when Deucalion and his Purrha hurl'd
2.14.20: The stones that sow'd with men the delug'd world,
2.14.21: Had Thetis, goddess of the sea, refus'd
2.14.22: To bear the burden, and her fruit abus'd,
2.14.23: Who would have Priam's royal seat destroy'd?
2.14.24: Or had the vestal whom fierce Mars enjoy'd,
2.14.25: Stifled the twins within her pergnant womb,
2.14.26: What founder would have then been born to Rome?
2.14.27: Had Venus, when she with Aeneas teem'd,
2.14.28: To death, ere born, Anchises' son condemn'd,
2.14.29: The world had of the Caesars been depriv'd;
2.14.30: Augustus ne'er had reign'd, nor Julius liv'd.
2.14.31: And thou, whose beauty is the boast of fame,
2.14.32: Hadst perish'd, had thy mother done the same;
2.14.33: Nor had I liv'd love's faithful slave to be,
2.14.34: Had my own mother dealt as ill by me.
2.14.35: Ah, vile invention, ah, accurs'd design,
2.14.36: To rob of rip'ning fruit the loaded vine
2.14.37: Ah, let it grow for nature's use mature,
2.14.38: Ah, let it its full length of time endure;
2.14.39: 'Twill of itself, alas! too soon decay,
2.14.40: And quickly fall, like autumn leaves, away
2.14.41: Why barb'rously dost thou thy bowels tear
2.14.42: To kill the human load that quickens there?
2.14.43: On venom'd drugs why venture, to destroy
2.14.44: The pledge of pleasure past, the promis'd boy?
2.14.45: Medea, guilty of her childrens' blood,
2.14.46: The mark of ev'ry age's curse has stood;
2.14.47: And Atys, murder'd by his mothers rage,
2.14.48: Been pitied since by each succeeding age;
2.14.49: Thy cruel parents by false lords abus'd,
2.14.50: Had yet some plea, tho' none their crime excus'd.
2.14.51: What, Jason, did your dire revenge provoke?
2.14.52: What, Tereus, urge you to the fatal stroke?
2.14.53: What rage your reason led so far away,
2.14.54: As furious hands upon yourself to lay?
2.14.55: The tigresses that haunt th' Armenian wood,
2.14.56: Will spare their proper young, though pinch'd for food;
2.14.57: Nor will the Libyan lionesses slay
2.14.58: Their whelps,—but woman are more fierce than they;
2.14.59: More barb'rous to the tender fruit they bear,
2.14.60: Nor nature's call, tho' loud she cries, will hear.
2.14.61: But righteous vengeance oft their crimes pursues,
2.14.62: And they are lost themselves, who would their
2.14.64: The pois'nous drugs with mortal juices fill
2.14.65: Their veins, and, undesign'd, themselves they kill
2.14.66: Themselves upon the bier are breathless borne,
2.14.67: With hair tied up that was in ringlets worn,
2.14.68: Thro' weeping crowds that on their course attend;
2.14.69: Well may they weep for their unhappy end.
2.14.70: Forbid it, heaven, that what I say may prove
2.14.71: Presaging to the fair I blame and love;
2.14.72: Thus let me ne'er, ye pow'rs, her death deplore,
2.14.73: 'Twas her first fault, and she'll offend no more;
2.14.74: No pardon she'll deserve a second time,
2.14.75: But, without mercy, punish then her crime.

2.15.1: Go, happy ring, who art about to bind
2.15.2: The fair one's finger; may the fair be kind.
2.15.3: Small is the present, tho' the love be great;
2.15.4: May she swift slip thee on thy taper seat.
2.15.5: As she and I, may thou with her agree,
2.15.6: And not too large, nor yet too little be.
2.15.7: To touch her hand thou wilt the pleasure have;
2.15.8: I now must envy what myself I gave.
2.15.9: O! would a Proteus or a Circe change
2.15.10: Me to thy form, that I like thee might range!
2.15.11: Then would I wish thee with her breasts to play,
2.15.12: And her left hand beneath her robes to stray.
2.15.13: Tho' straight she thought me, I will then appear
2.15.14: Loose and unfix'd, and slip I know not where.
2.15.15: Whene'er she writes some secret lines of love,
2.15.16: Lest the dry gum and wax should sticking prove,
2.15.17: He first she moistens: then sly care I take,
2.15.18: And but, when lines I like, impression make.
2.15.19: Of in her pocket fain she would me hide,
2.15.20: Close will I press her finger, and not slide;
2.15.21: Then cry, "My life, I ne'er shall thee disgrace,
2.15.22: And I am light; give me my proper place.
2.15.23: Still let me stick when in the bath you are;
2.15.24: If I catch damage,'tis not worth your care.
2.15.25: Yea, when the ring thy naked body spies,
2.15.26: It will transform, and I a man arise."
2.15.27: Why do I rave? thou little trifle, go,
2.15.28: And that I die for her let the dear creature know.

2.16.1: I'm now at—where my eyes can view,
2.16.2: Their old delights, but what I want in you:
2.16.3: Here purling streams cut thro' my pleasing bowr's,
2.16.4: Adorn my banks, and raise my drooping flow'rs;
2.16.5: Here trees with bending fruit in order stand,
2.16.6: Invite my eye, and tempt my greedy hand;
2.16.7: But half the pleasure of enjoyment's gone;
2.16.8: Since I must pluck them single and alone;
2.16.9: Why could not nature's kindness first contrive,
2.16.10: That faithful lovers should like spirits live,
2.16.11: Mix'd in one point and yet divided lie,
2.16.13: But since we must thro' distant regions go,
2.16.14: Why was not the same way design'd for two?
2.16.15: One single care determined still for both,
2.16.16: And the kind virgin join'd the loving youth?
2.16.17: Then should I think it pleasant way to go
2.16.18: Oe'r Alpine frost, and trace the hills of snow;
2.16.19: Then should I dare to view the horrid moors,
2.16.20: And walk the deserts of the Libyan shores;
2.16.21: Hear Scylla bark, and see Charybdis rave,
2.16.22: Suck in and vomit out the threat'ning wave;
2.16.23: Fearless through all I'd steer my feeble barge,
2.16.24: Secure, and safe with the celestial charge,
2.16.25: But now, though here my grateful fields afford
2.16.26: Choice fruits to cheer their malancholy lord;
2.16.27: Though here obedient streams the gard'ner leads,
2.16.28: In narrow channels through my flow'ry beds;
2.16.29: The poplars rise, and spread a shady grove,
2.16.30: Where I might lie, my little life improve,
2.16.31: And spend my minutes 'twixt a muse and love:
2.16.32: Yet these contributes little to my ease,
2.16.33: For without you they lose the power to please;
2.16.34: I seem to walk oe'r the fields of naked sand,
2.16.35: Or tread an antic maze in fairy land,
2.16.36: Where frightful specires, and pale shades appear,
2.16.37: And hollow groans invade my troubled ear;
2.16.38: Where ev'ry breeze that through my arbour flies,
2.16.39: First sadly murmurs, and then turns to sighs.
2.16.40: The vines love elms; what elms from vines remove?
2.16.41: Then why should I be parted from my love?
2.16.42: And yet by me you once devoutly swore,
2.16.43: By your own eyes, those stars that I adore,
2.16.44: That all my bus'ness you would make your own,
2.16.45: And never suffer me to be alone:
2.16.47: Their frequent oaths are like the falling leaves,
2.16.48: Which when a storm has from the branches tore
2.16.49: Are lost by ev'ry blast, and seen no more:
2.16.50: Yet if you will be true, your vows retrieve,
2.16.51: Be kind, and I can easily forgive;
2.16.52: Prepare your coach, to me direct your course,
2.16.53: Drive fiercely on, and lash the lazy horse;
2.16.54: And while you ride I will prolong the day,
2.16.55: And try the power of verse to smooth your way.
2.16.56: Sink down ye mountains, sink ye lofty hills,
2.16.57: Ye vallies be obedient to her wheels,
2.16.58: Ye streams be dry, ye hindr'ing woods remove,
2.16.59: 'Tis love that drives, and all must yield to love!

2.17.1:
Corinna he will always be her slave
If there's a wretch, who thinks it is a shame,
2.17.2: To serve a lovely and a loving dame:
2.17.3: If such a slave he loads with infamy,
2.17.4: I'm willing he should judge as hard of me;
2.17.5: I'm willing all the world should know my shame
2.17.6: If Venus will abate my raging flame.
2.17.7: Let me a fair and gentle mistress have,
2.17.8: And then proclaim aloud that I'm her slave.
2.17.9: Beauty is apt to swell a maiden's mind,
2.17.10: And thus Corinna is to pride inclin'd:
2.17.11: But as she is above all maiden's fair,
2.17.12: What's pride in them is insolence in her;
2.17.13: Less fair I wish she was, or knew it less;
2.17.14: How learnt she, she is lovely by her face!
2.17.15: Her mirror tells her so, she often tries
2.17.16: Her mirror, and believes her charming eyes.
2.17.17: The looks she then puts on, are still her best,
2.17.18: And she ne'er uses it but when she's dress'd.
2.17.19: Though wide the empire of your beauties spread,
2.17.20: Beauty to draw my am'rous glances made:
2.17.21: Compare your servant's merit with your eyes,
2.17.22: You'll find no cause his service to dispise.
2.17.23: Don't think I press upon your pride too hard.
2.17.24: For little things may be with great compar'd:
2.17.25: We're told Calypso, an immortal pow'r,
2.17.26: Detain'd a mortal in th' Ogygian pow'r,
2.17.27: And when her pray'r to stay he would not grant,
2.17.28: So strong her love, she kept him by constraint.
2.17.29: A Nereid took the Pythian to her arms.
2.17.30: And Numa knew divine Egeria's charms.
2.17.31: Vulcan though lame, and of a form obscene,
2.17.32: Was oft made happy by the Paphian queen;
2.17.33: She matter'd not his limping, but approv'd
2.17.34: His flame, and saw no faults in him she lov'd
2.17.35: My verses are unequal like his feet,
2.17.36: Yet the long kindly with the shorter meet.
2.17.37: As they with them, why shouldst thou not with me
2.17.38: Comply, my life and my divinity!
2.17.39: Myself, when I am in thy arms, I'll own
2.17.40: Thy subject, and the bed shall be thy throne;
2.17.41: Thou there, my lovely queen, shall give me laws,
2.17.42: Nor in my absence, to rejoice have cause,
2.17.43: Nor ever shall my services be blam'd
2.17.44: Nor shalt thou of thy servant be asham'd.
2.17.45: My poetry's my purse, my fortun's there,
2.17.46: I have no other way to win the fair;
2.17.47: Nor is that way the worst; the brightest dames
2.17.48: Would in my verse immortalize their names.
2.17.49: My muse the place of an estate supplies,
2.17.50: And none that know her worth, her wealth despise.
2.17.51: Some tempted by Corinna's spreading fame,
2.17.52: In envy rob her, and usurp her name;
2.17.53: What would they give, d'ye think, to be the same?
