Or barb'rous beauties of the Parthian race.
Ungraceful 'tis to see without a horn
The lofty hart whom branches best adorn,
A leafless tree, or an unverdant mead,
And as ungraceful is a hairless head.
But think not these instructions are design'd
For first-rate beauties of the finish'd kind;
Not to a Semele, or a Leda bright,
Nor an Europa, these my rules I write;
Nor the fair Helen do I teach, whose charms
Stirr'd up Atrides and all Greece to arms;
Thee to regain well was that war begun,
And Paris well defended what he won:
What lover or what husband would not fight
In such a cause, where both are in the right?
3.257:
The crowd I teach, some homely and some fair,
But of the former sort the larger share.
The handsome least require the help of art,
Rich in themselves, and pleas'd with nature's part.
When calm the sea, at ease the pilot lies,
But all his skill exerts when storms arise.
Faults in your person or your face correct;
And few are seen that have not some defect.
The nymph too short her seat should seldom quit,
Lest when she stands she may be thought to sit;
And when extended on her couch she lies,
Let length of petticoats conceal her size.
The lean of thick wrought stuff her clothes should choose,
And fuller made than what the plumper use.
If pale, let her the crimson juice apply;
If swarthy, to the Pharian varnish fly.
A leg too lank tight garters still must wear,
Nor should an ill-shap'd foot be ever bare.
Round shoulders, bolster'd, will appear the least;
And lacing straight confines too full a breast.
Whose fingers are too fat, and nails too coarse,
Should always shun much gesture in discourse;
And you whose breath is touch'd, this caution take,
Nor fasting, nor too near another, speak.
Let not the nymph with laughter much abound,
Whose teeth are black, uneven, or unsound.
You'd hardly think how much on this depends,
And how a laugh or spoils a face or mends.
Gape not too wide, lest you disclose your gums,
And lose the dimple which the cheek becomes.
Nor let your sides too long concussions shake,
Lest you the softness of the sex forsake:
In some, distortions quite the face disguise;
Another laughs, that you would think she cries.
In one, too hoarse a voice we hear betray'd;
Another's is as harsh as if she bray'd.
What cannot art attain! Many, with ease,
Have learn'd to weep, both when and how they please.
Others thro' affectation lisp; and find
In imperfection charms to catch mankind.
Neglect no means which may promote your end;
Now learn what way of walking recommends.
Too masculine a motion shocks the sight;
But female grace allures with strange delight.
One has an artful swing and jut behind,
Which helps her coats to catch the swelling wind;
Swell'd with the wanton wind, they loosely flow,
And ev'ry step and graceful motion show.
Another, like an Umbrian's sturdy spouse,
Strides all the space her petticoats allows.
Between extremes, in this, a mean adjust,
Nor show too nice a gait, nor too robust.
If snowy white your neck, you still should wear
That, and the shoulder of the left arm bare;
Such sights ne'er fail to fire my am'rous heart,
And make me pant to kiss the naked part.
3.311:
Sirens, tho' monsters of the stormy main,
Can ships, when under sail, with songs detain:
Scarce could Ulysses by his friends be bound,
When first he listen'd to the charming sound,
Singing insinuates, learn all ye maids;
Oft when a face forbids, a voice persuades.
Whether on theatres loud strains we hear,
Or in Ruelles some soft Egyptian air.
Well shall she sing, of whom I make my choice,
And with her lute accompany her voice.
The rocks were stirr'd, the beasts to listen staid
When on his lyre melodious Orpheus play'd,
Even Cerberus and hell that sound obey'd,
And stones officious were thy walls to raise.
0, Thebes, attracted by Amphion's lays.
The dolphin, dumb itself, thy voice admir'd,
And was, Arion, by thy songs inspir'd.
Of sweet Callimachus the works rehearse,
And real Philetas and Anacreon's verse,
Terentian plays may much the mind improve;
But softest Sappho best instructs to love.
Propertius, Gallus, and Tibullus read,
And let Varronian verse to these succeed.
Then mighty Maro's work with care peruse;
Of all the Latians boards the noblest muse,
Even I, 'tis possible, in after-days,
May 'scape oblivion, and be nam'd with these.
My labour'd lines, some readers may approve,
Since I've instructed either sex in love.
Whatever book you read of this soft art,
Read with a lover's voice and lover's heart.
Tender epistles too, by me are fram'd,
A work before unthought of, and unnam'd.
Such was your sacred will, 0, tuneful nine!
Such thine Apollo, and Lycreus, thine!
Still unaccomplish'd may the maid be thought,
Who gracefully to dance was never taught:
That active dancing may to love engage,
Witness the well-kept dancers of the stage.
3.353:
Of some odd trifles I'm asham'd to tell,
Tho' it becomes the sex to trifle well;
To raffle prettily, or slur a die,
Implies both cunning and dexterity;
Nor is't amiss at chess to be expert,
For games most thoughtful, sometimes most divert.
Learn ev'ry game, you'll find it prove of use;
Parties begun at play may love produce:
But easier 'tis to learn how bets to lay,
Than how to keep your temper while you play.
Unguarded then, each breast is open laid,
And while the head's intent, the heart's betray'd.
Then base desire of gain, then rage appears,
Quarrels and brawls arise, and anxious fears;
Then clamours and revilings reach the sky,
While losing gamsters all the gods defy.
They grieve, and curse, and storm, nay weep at last.
Good Jove avert such shameful faults as these,
From ev'ry nymph whose heart's inclin'd to please
Soft recreations fit the female kind;
Nature, for men, has rougher sports design'd:
To wield the sword and hurl the pointed spear;
To stop or turn the steed in full career.
Tho' martial fields ill suit your tender frames,
Nor may you swim in Tiber's rapid streams;
Yet when Sol's burning wheels from Leo drive,
And at the glowing Virgin's sign arrive,
'Tis both allow'd and fit you should repair,
To pleasant walks, and breathe refreshing air.
To Pompey's gardens, or the shady groves
Which Caesar honours, and which Phoebus loves:
Phoebus, who sunk the proud Egyptian fleet,
And made Augustus' victory complete.
Or seek those shades, where monuments of fame
Are raised to Livia's or Octavia's name;
Or where Agrippa first adorn'd the ground,
When he with naval victory was crown'd.
To Isis' fine, to theatres resort;
And in the circus see the noble sport.
In ev'ry public place, by turns be shown;
In vain you're fair while you remain unknown.
Should you in singing, Thamyras transcend;
Your voice unheard, who will your skill commend!
Had not Appelles drawn the sea-born queen,
Her beauties still beneath the waves had been.
Poets inspir'd write only for a name,
And think their labours well repay'd with fame.
In former days, I own, the poets were
Of gods and king the most peculiar care:
Majestic awe was in the name allow'd,
And they with rich possessions were endowed
Ennius with honours was by Scipio grac'd,
And next his own the poets statue plac'd.
But now their ivy crowns bear no esteem,
And all their learning's thought an idle dream.
Still there's a pleasure that proceeds from praise:
What could the high renown of Homer raise,
But that he sung his Iliad's deathless lays?
3.415:
Who could have been of Danae's charms assur'd,
Had she grown old, within her tow'r immur'd?
This, as a rule, let ev'ry nymph pursue,
That 'tis her int'rest oft' to come in view.
A hungry wolf at all the herd will run,
In hopes, through many, to make sure of one.
So, let the fair the gazing crowd assail,
That over one, at least, she may prevail.
In ev'ry place to please, be all her thought;
Where, sometimes, least we think, the fish is caught.
Sometimes, all day, we hunt the tedious foil,
Anon, the stag himself shall seek the toil.
How could Andromeda once doubt relief,
Whose charms were heighten'd and adorn'd by grief?
The widow'd fair, who sees her lord expire,
While yet she weeps, may kindle new desire,
And Hymen's torch relight the fun'ral fire.
Beware of men who are too sprucely dress'd;
And look, you fly with speed a fop profess'd.
Such tools to you, and to a thousand more,
Will tell the same dull story o'er and o'er.
This way add that, unsteadily they rove,
And never fixed, are fugitives in love.
Such flutt'ring things all women sure should hate,
Light as themselves, and more effeminate.
Believe me, all I say is for your good;
Had Priam been believ'd, Troy still had stood.
Many, with base designs, will passions feign,
Who know no love, but sordid love of gain.
But let not powder'd heads, nor essenc'd hair,
Your well-believing, easy hearts ensnare.
Rich clothes are oft by common sharpers worn,
And diamond rings felonious hands adorn.
So may your lover burn with fierce desire
Your jewels to enjoy, and best attire.
Poor Chloe robb'd, runs crying thro' the streets;
And as she runs," Give me my own," repeats.
How often, Venus, hast thou heard such cries,
And laugh'd amidst thy Appian votaries?
Some, so notorious are their very name,
Must ev'ry nymph whom they frequent defame.
Be warn'd by ills which others have destroy'd,
And faithless men with constant care avoid.
Trust not a Theseus, fair Athenian maid,
Who has so oft th' attesting gods betray'd.
And thou, Demophoon, heir to Theseus' crimes,
Hast lost thy credit to all future times.
3.461:
Promise for promise equally afford,
But once a contract made, keep well your word.
For she for any act of hell is fit,
And undismayed may sacrilege commit;
With impious hands could quench the vestal fire
Poison her husband in her arms for hire,
Who first to take a lover's gift complies,
And then defrauds him, and his claim denies.
But hold, my muse, check thy unruly horse,
And more in sight pursue th' intended course.
If love epistles tender lines impart,
And billet-doux are sent to sound your heart,
Let all such letters by a faithful maid,
Or confident, be secretly convey'd.
Soon from the words you'll judge, if read with care,
When feign'd a passion is, and when sincere.
Ere in return you write some time require;
Delays, if not too long, increase desire;
Nor let the pressing youth with ease obtain,
Nor yet refuse him with too rude disdain.
Now let his hopes, now let his fears increase,
But by degrees, let fear to hope give place.
Be sure avoid set phrases when you write,
The usual way of speech is more polite.
How have I seen the puzzl'd lover vex'd,
To read a letter with hard words perplex'd;
A style too coarse takes from a handsome face,
And makes us wish an uglier in its place.
But since (tho' chastity be not your care)
You from your husband still would hide th' affair,
Write to no stranger till his truth be tried;
Nor in a foolish messenger confide.
What agonies that woman undergoes,
Whose hand the traitor threatens to expose;
Who rashly trusting, dreads to be deceiv'd,
And lives for ever to that dread enslav'd!
Such treachery can never be surpass'd,
For those discoveries, sure as light'ning, blast.
Might I advise, fraud shou'd with fraud be paid;
Let arms repel all who with arms invade.
3.76: Lest you too soon your new admirer fright.
3.555:
As skilful riders rein, with diff'rent force,
A new-back'd courser and a well-train'd horse,
Do you by diffrent management engage
The man in years, and youth of greener age.
This, while the wiles of love are yet unknown,
Will gladly cleave to you, and you alone;
With kind caresses oft indulge the boy,
And all the harvest of his heart enjoy.
Alone, thus bless'd, of rivals most beware;
Nor love nor empire can a partner bear.
Men more discreetly love, when more mature,
And many things, which youth disdains, endure;
No windows break, nor houses set on fire,
Nor tear their own, or mistress's attire.
In youth, the boiling blood gives fury vent,
But men in years more calmly wrong resent;
As wood when green, or as a torch when wet,
They slowly burn, but long retain their heat.
More bright is youthful flame, but sooner dies;
Then swiftly seize the joy that swiftly flies.
Thus, all betraying to the beauteous foe,
How surely to enslave ourselves we show.
To trust a traitor you'll no scruple make,
Who is a traitor only for your sake.
Who yields too soon will soon her lover lose;
Would you retain him long? then long refuse.
Oft at your door make him for entrance wait;
There let him lie, and threaten and entreat.
When cloy'd with sweets, bitters the taste restore;
Ships by fair winds are sometimes run ashore;
Hence springs the coldness in a married life;
The husband when he pleases has his wife.
Bar but your gate, and let your porter cry,
"Here's no admittance, sir; I must deny;"
The very husband, — so repuls'd, will find
A growing inclination to be kind.
3.589:
Thus far with foils you've sought those laid aside;
I now sharp weapons for the sex provide,
Nor doubt not 'gainst myself to see 'em tried.
When first a lover you design to charm,
Beware lest jealousies his soul alarm;
Make him believe with all the skill you can,
That he and only he's the happy man.
Anon, by due degrees, small doubts create,
And let him fear some rival's better fate.
Such little arts make love its vigour hold,
Which else would languish, and too soon grow old.
Then strains the courser to outstrip the wind,
When one before him runs, and one he hears behind.
Love, when extinct, suspicions may revive;
I own when mine's secure 'tis scarce alive.
Yet no precaution to this rule belongs;
Let us at most suspect, not prove our wrongs.
Sometimes your lover, to incite the more,
Pretends your husband's spies beset the door;
Tho' free as Thais, still affect a fright,
For seeming danger heightens the delight.
Oft let the youth in thro' your windows steal,
Tho' he might enter at the door as well;
And sometimes let your maid surprise pretend,
And beg you in some hole to hide your friend:
Yet ever and anon dispel his fear,
And let him taste of happiness sincere;
Lest, quite dishearten'd with too much fatigue,
He should grow weary of the dull intrigue.
But I forgot to tell how you may try
Both to evade the husband and the spy.
That wives should of their husbands stand in awe,
Agrees with justice, modesty, and law;
But that a mistress may be lawful prize,
None but her keeper I am sure denies.
For such fair nymphs these precepts are design'd,
Which ne'er can fail, join'd with a willing mind.
Tho' stuck with Argus' eyes your keeper were,
Advis'd by me you shall elude his care.
When you to wash or bathe retire from eight,
Can he observe what letters then you write?
Or can his caution against such provide,
Which in her breast your confidant may hide!
Can he that note beneath her garter view,
Or that which more conceal'd is in her shoe?
Yet, these perceived, you may her back undress,
And writing on her skin your mind express.
New milk, or pointed spires of flax when green,
Will ink supply, and letters mark unseen.
Fair will the paper, show, nor can be read,
Till all the writing 's with warm ashes spread.
Acresius was with all his care betray'd,
And in his tow'r of brass a grandsire made.
3.633:
Can spies avail when you to plays resort,
Or in the circus view the noble sport?
Or can you be to Isis' fane pursu'd,
Or Cybele's, whose rights all men exclude?
Tho' watchful servants to the Bagnio come,
They're ne'er admitted to the bathing-room.
Or when some sudden sickness you pretend,
May you not take to your sick bed a friend?
False keys a private passage may procure,
If not, there are more ways besides the door.
Sometimes with wine your watchful follower treat;
When drunk, you may with ease his care defeat:
Or, to prevent too sudden a surprise,
Prepare a sleeping draught to seal his eyes;
Or let your maid, still longer time to gain,
An inclination for his person feign;
With faint resistance let her drill him on,
And, after competent delays, be won.
But what need all these various doubtful wiles,
Since gold the greatest vigilance beguiles?
Believe me, men and gods with gifts are pleas'd,
E'en angry Jove with offerings is appeas'd;
With presents fools and wise alike are caught;
Give but enough, the husband may be bought,
But let we warn you, when you bribe a spy,
That you for ever his connivance buy;
Pay him his price at once, for with such men
You'll know no end of giving now and then.
Once, I remember, I with cause complain'd
Of jealousy occasion'd by a friend.
Believe me, apprehensions of that kind
Are not alone to our false sex confin'd.
Trust not too far your she-companion's truth,
Lest she sometimes should intercept the youth;
The very confidant that lends the bed,
May entertain your lover in your stead.
Nor keep a servant with too fair a face,
For such I've known supply her lady's place.
But whither do I run with heedless rage,
Teaching the foe unequal war to wage?
Did ever bird the fowler's net prepare?
Was ever hound instructed by the hare?
But all self-ends and int'rests set apart,
I'll faithfully proceed to teach my art;
Defenceless and unarm'd expose my life,
And for the Lemnian ladies whet the knife.
Perpetual fondness of your lover feign,
Nor will you find it hard belief to gain;
Full of himself, he your design will aid!
To what we wish 'tis easy to persuade.
With dying eyes his face and form survey,
Then sigh, and wonder he so long could stay;
Now, drop a tear your sorrows to assuage,
Anon, reproach him, and pretend to rage.
Such proofs as these will all distrust remove,
And make him pity your excessive love.
Scarce to himself will he forbear to cry,
"How can I let this poor fond creature die?"
But chiefly one such fond behaviour fires,
Who courts his glass, and his own charms admires.
Proud of the homage to his merit done,
He'll think a goddess might with ease be won.
Light wrongs be sure you still with mildness bear,
Nor straight fly out when you a rival fear.
Let not your passions o'er your sense prevail,
Nor credit lightly ev'ry idle tale.
Let Procris' fate a sad example be
Of what effects attend credulity.
3.747:
Now to pursue our voyage we must provide,
Till safe to port our weary bark we guide.
You may expect, perhaps, I now should teach
What rules to treats and entertainments reach.
Come not the first, invited to a feast;
Rather come last, as a more grateful guest,
For that of which we fear to be depriv'd,
Meets with the surest welcome when arriv'd.
Besides, complexions of a coarser kind,
From candle-light no small advantage find.
During the time you eat, observe some grace,
Nor let your unwip'd hands besmear your face;
Nor yet too squeamishly your meat avoid,
Lest we suspect you were in private cloy'd.
Of all extremes in either kind forbear
And still, before your belly's full, beware.
No glutton nymph, however fair, can wound,
Tho' more than Helen she in charms abound.
I own I think of wire the moderate use
More suits the sex, and sooner finds excuse;
It warms the blood, adds lustre to the eyes,
And wine and love have always been allies.
But carefully from all intemperance keep,
Nor drink till you see double, lisp, or sleep;
For in such sleeps brutalities are done,
Which, tho' you loath, you have no pow'r to shun.
And now th' instructed nymph from table led,
Should next be taught how to behave in bed;—
But modesty forbids: nor more my muse
With weary wings the labour'd flight pursues;
Her purple swans unyok'd, the chariot leave,
And needful rest (their journey done) receive.
Thus, with impartial care, my art I show,
And equal arms on either sex bestow;
White men and maids, who by my rules improve,
Ovid, must own, their master is in love.

Where Bacchus was, and why they had not done as he commaunded.
Consistes the savegard of us all. And wyth that word he takes
3.85:
Save that he left the head therof among his bones behinde.
His houndes espyde him where he was, and Blackfoote first of all
Was burned in hir Lovers armes. But yet he tooke away
The Goddesse Ramnuse (who doth wreake on wicked people take)
He goes me to the Well of Styx, and there both day and night
Sir (aunswerde they) we saw him not, but this same fellow heere
My roume, and leaving Naxus quite to other countries makes.
3.86:
When of his courage through the wound more kindled was the ire,
And Stalker speciall good of scent began aloud to call.
His infant from the mothers wombe unperfect as it lay,
Assented to his just request for ruth and pities sake.
Standes tooting on his shadow still as fondely as before.
A chiefe companion in his traine and worker in this geere,
The God then dalying with these mates, as though he had at last
3.87:
His throteboll swelde with puffed veines, his eyes gan sparkle fire.
This latter was a hounde of Crete, the other was of Spart.
And (if a man may credit it) did in his thigh it sowe,
There was a spring withouten mudde as silver cleare and still,
The water Nymphes, his sisters, wept and wayled for him sore
Wee tooke by force: and therewithall presented to their Lord
Begon to smell their suttle craft, out of the foredecke cast
3.88:
There stoode about his smeared chaps a lothly foming froth.
Then all the kenell fell in round, and everie for his part,
Where byding out the mothers tyme it did to ripenesse growe.
Which neyther sheepeheirds, nor the Goates that fed upon the hill,
And on his bodie strowde their haire clipt off and shorne therefore.
A certaine man of Tirrhene lande, his handes fast bound with cord,
His eye upon the Sea: and then as though he seemde to weepe,
3.89:
His skaled brest ploughes up the ground, the stinking breath that goth
Dyd follow freshly in the chase more swifter than the winde,
And when the time of birth was come his Aunt the Ladie Ine
Nor other cattell troubled had, nor savage beast had styrd,
The Wood nymphes also did lament. And Echo did rebound
Whome they, frequenting Bacchus rites had found but late before.
Sayd: Sirs, to bring me on this coast ye doe not promise keepe.
3.90:
Out from his blacke and hellish mouth infectes the herbes full fowle.
Spy, Eateal, Scalecliffe, three good houndes comne all of Arcas kinde,
Did nourse him for a while by stealth and kept him trym and fine.
Nor braunch nor sticke, nor leafe of tree, nor any soule nor byrd.
To every sorrowfull noyse of theirs with like lamenting sound.
A grim and cruell looke which yre did make to seeme more sore,
I see that this is not the land the which I did request.
3.91:
Sometime he windes himselfe in knots as round as any Bowle.
Strong Bilbucke, currish Savage, Spring, and Hunter fresh of smell,
The Nymphes of Nysa afterwarde did in their bowres him hide,
The moysture fed and kept aye fresh the grasse that grew about,
The fire was made to burne the corse, and waxen Tapers light.
Did Penthey cast upon the man. And though he scarcely stayd
For what occasion in this sort deserve I to be drest?
3.92:
Sometime he stretcheth out in length as straight as any beame.
And Lightfoote who to lead a chase did beare away the bell,
And brought him up with Milke till tyme he might abrode be spyde.
And with their leaves the trees did keepe the heate of Phoebus out.
A Herce to lay the bodie on with solemne pompe was dight.
From putting him to tormentes strait, O wretched man (he sayde)
What commendation can you win, or praise thereby receyve,
3.93:
Anon againe with violent brunt he rusheth like a streame
Fierce Woodman hurte not long ago in hunting of a Bore,
The stripling wearie with the heate and hunting in the chace,
But as for bodie none remaind: in stead thereof they found
Who by thy worthie death shalt be a sample unto other,
If men a Lad, if many one ye compasse to deceyve?
3.94:
Encreast by rage of latefalne raine, and with his mightie sway
And Shepeheird woont to follow sheepe and neate to fielde afore.
And much delighted with the spring and coolenesse of the place,
A yellow floure with milke white leaves new sprong upon the ground.
Declare to me the names of thee, thy father and thy mother,
I wept and sobbed all this while, the wicked villaines laught,
3.95:
Beares downe the wood before his breast that standeth in his way.
And Laund, a fell and eger bitch that had a Wolfe to Syre:
Did lay him downe upon the brim: and as he stooped lowe
And in what Countrie thou wert borne, and what hath caused thee,
And rowed forth with might and maine, as though they had bene straught.
3.96:
Agenors sonne retiring backe doth with his Lions spoyle
Another brach callde Greedigut with two hir Puppies by her.
To staunche his thurst, another thurst of worse effect did growe.
Of these straunge rites and sacrifice, a follower for to bee.
Now even by him (for sure than he in all the worlde so wide
3.97:
Defend him from his fierce assaults, and makes him to recoyle
And Ladon gant as any Greewnd, a hownd in Sycion bred,
For as he dranke, he chaunst to spie the Image of his face,
There is no God more neare at hand at every time and tide)
3.98:
Aye holding at the weapons point. The Serpent waxing wood
Blab, Fleetewood, Patch whose flecked skin with sundrie spots was spred:
The which he did immediately with fervent love embrace.
I sweare unto you that the things the which I shall declare,
3.99:
Doth crashe the steele betwene his teeth, and bites it till the blood,
Wight, Bowman, Royster, Beautie faire and white as winters snow,
He feedes a hope without cause why. For like a foolishe noddie
Like as they seeme incredible, even so most true they are.
3.100:
Dropt mixt with poyson from his mouth, did die the greene grasse blacke,
And Tawnie full of duskie haires that over all did grow,
He thinkes the shadow that he sees, to be a lively boddie.
The ship stoode still amid the Sea as in a dustie docke.
3.101:
But yet the wound was verie light bicause he writhed backe
With lustie Ruffler passing all the resdue there in strength,
Astraughted like an ymage made of Marble stone he lyes,
They wondring at this miracle, and making but a mocke,
3.102:
And puld his head still from the stroke: and made the stripe to die
And Tempest best of footemanshipe in holding out at length.
There gazing on his shadowe still with fixed staring eyes.
Persist in beating with their Ores, and on with all their sayles.
3.103:
By giving way, untill that Cadmus following irefully
And Cole and Swift, and little Woolfe, as wight as any other,
Stretcht all along upon the ground, it doth him good to see
To make their Galley to remove, no Art nor labor fayles.
3.104:
The stroke, with all his powre and might did through the throte him rive,
Accompanide with a Ciprian hound that was his native brother,
His ardant eyes which like two starres full bright and shyning bee,
But Ivie troubled so their Ores that forth they could not row:
3.105:
And naylde him to an Oke behind the which he eke did clive.
And Snatch amid whose forehead stoode a starre as white as snowe,
And eke his fingars, fingars such as Bacchus might beseeme,
And both with Beries and with leaves their sailes did overgrow.
3.106:
The Serpents waight did make the tree to bend. It grievde the tree
The resdue being all as blacke and slicke as any Crowe.
And haire that one might worthely Apollos haire it deeme,
And he himselfe with clustred grapes about his temples round,
3.107:
His bodie of the Serpents taile thus scourged for to bee.
And shaggie Rugge with other twaine that had a Syre of Crete,
His beardlesse chinne and yvorie necke, and eke the perfect grace
Did shake a Javeling in his hand that round about was bound
3.108:
And Dam of Sparta: T'one of them callde Jollyboy, a great
Of white and red indifferently bepainted in his face.
With leaves of Vines: and at his feete there seemed for to couch
3.109:
And large flewd hound: the tother Chorle who ever gnoorring went,
All these he woondreth to beholde, for which (as I doe gather)
Of Tygers, Lynx, and Panthers shapes most ougly for to touch.
3.110:
And Kingwood with a shyrle loude mouth the which he freely spent,
Himselfe was to be woondred at, or to be pitied rather.
I cannot tell you whether feare or woodnesse were the cause,
3.111:
With divers mo whose names to tell it were but losse of tyme.
He is enamored of himselfe for want of taking heede,
But every person leapeth up and from his labor drawes.
3.112:
This fellowes over hill and dale in hope of pray doe clyme.
And where he lykes another thing, he lykes himselfe in deede.
And there one Medon first of all began to waxen blacke,
3.113:
Through thicke and thin and craggie cliffes where was no way to go,
He is the partie whome he wooes, and suter that doth wooe,
And having lost his former shape did take a courbed backe.
3.114:
He flyes through groundes where oftentymes he chased had ere tho.
He is the flame that settes on fire, and thing that burneth tooe.
What Monster shall we have of thee (quoth Licab) and with that
3.115:
Even from his owne folke is he faine (alas) to flee away.
O Lord how often did he kisse that false deceitfull thing?
This Licabs chappes did waxen wide, his nosetrils waxed flat,
3.116:
He strayned oftentymes to speake, and was about to say:
How often did he thrust his armes midway into the spring
His skin waxt tough, and scales thereon began anon to grow.
3.117:
I am Acteon: know your Lorde and Mayster, sirs, I pray.
To have embraste the necke he saw and could not catch himselfe?
And Libis as he went about the Ores away to throw,
3.118:
But use of wordes and speach did want to utter forth his minde.
He knowes not what it was he sawe. And yet the foolish elfe
Perceived how his hands did shrinke and were become so short,
3.119:
Their crie did ring through all the Wood redoubled with the winde,
Doth burne in ardent love thereof. The verie selfsame thing
That now for finnes and not for hands he might them well report.
3.120:
First Slo did pinch him by the haunch, and next came Kildeere in,
That doth bewitch and blinde his eyes, encreaseth all his sting.
Another as he would have claspt his arme about the corde:
3.121:
And Hylbred fastned on his shoulder, bote him through the skinne.
Thou fondling thou, why doest thou raught the fickle image so?
Had nere an arme, and so bemaimd in bodie, over boord
3.122:
These cam forth later than the rest, but coasting thwart a hill,
The thing thou seekest is not there. And if aside thou go,
He leapeth downe among the waves, and forked is his tayle
3.123:
They did gainecope him as he came, and helde their Master still
The thing thou lovest straight is gone. It is none other matter
As are the homes of Phebes face when halfe hir light doth fayle.
3.124:
Untill that all the rest came in, and fastned on him too.
That thou doest see, than of thy selfe the shadow in the water.
They leape about and sprinkle up much water on the ship,
3.125:
No part of him was free from wound. He could none other do
The thing is nothing of it selfe: with thee it doth abide,
One while they swim above, and downe againe anon they slip.
3.126:
But sigh, and in the shape of Hart with voyce as Hartes are woont,
With thee it would departe if thou withdrew thy selfe aside.
They fetch their friskes as in a daunce, and wantonly they writhe
3.127:
(For voyce of man was none now left to helpe him at the brunt)
Now here now there among the waves their bodies bane and lithe.
3.128:
By braying shew his secret grief among the Mountaynes hie,
And with their wide and hollow nose the water in they snuffe,
3.129:
And kneeling sadly on his knees with dreerie teares in eye,
And by their noses out againe as fast they doe it puffe.
3.130:
As one by humbling of himselfe that mercy seemde to crave,
Of twentie persons (for our ship so many men did beare)
3.131:
With piteous looke in stead of handes his head about to wave.
I only did remaine nigh straught and trembling still for feare.
3.132:
Not knowing that it was their Lord, the huntsmen cheere their houndsi
The God could scarce recomfort me, and yet he said: Go too,
3.133:
With wonted noyse and for Acteon looke about the grounds.
Feare not but saile to Dia ward. His will I gladly doe.
3.134:
They hallow who could lowdest crie still calling him by name,
And so as soone as I came there with right devout intent,
3.135:
As though he were not there, and much his absence they do blame
His Chaplaine I became. And thus his Orgies I frequent.
3.136: In that he came not to the fall, but slackt to see the game.
3.137: As often as they named him he sadly shooke his head,
3.138: And faine he would have beene away thence in some other stead.
3.139: But there he was. And well he could have found in heart to see
3.140: His dogges fell deedes, so that to feele in place he had not bee.
3.141: They hem him in on everie side, and in the shape of Stagge,
3.142: With greedie teeth and griping pawes their Lord in peeces dragge.
3.143: So fierce was cruell Phoebes wrath, it could not be alayde,
3.144: Till of his fault by bitter death the raunsome he had payde.
3.314:
Now while these things were done on earth, and that by fatal doome
The twice borne Bacchus had a tyme to mannes estate to come,
They say that Jove disposde to myrth as he and Juno sate
A drinking Nectar after meate in sport and pleasant rate,
Did fall a jeasting with his wife, and saide: A greater pleasure
In Venus games ye women have than men beyonde all measure.
She answerde no. To trie the truth, they both of them agree
The wise Tyresias in this case indifferent Judge to bee,
Who both the man and womans joyes by tryall understood.
For finding once two mightie Snakes engendring in a Wood,
He strake them overthwart the backs, by meanes whereof beholde
(As straunge a thing to be of truth as ever yet was tolde)
He being made a woman straight, seven winter lived so.
The eight he finding them againe did say unto them tho:
And if to strike ye have such powre as for to turne their shape
That are the givers of the stripe, before you hence escape,
One stripe now will I lende you more. He strake them as beforne
And straight returnd his former shape in which he first was borne.
Tyresias therefore being tane to judge this jesting strife,
Gave sentence on the side of Jove. The which the Queene his wife
Did take a great deale more to heart than needed, and in spight
To wreake hir teene upon hir Judge, bereft him of his sight.
But Jove (for to the Gods it is unleefull to undoe
The things which other of the Gods by any meanes have doe)
Did give him sight in things to come for losse of sight of eye,
And so his grievous punishment with honour did supplie.
3.690:
Thou makste a processe verie long (quoth Penthey) to th'intent
That (choler being coolde by time) mine anger might relent.
But Sirs (he spake it to his men) go take him by and by,
With cruell torments out of hand goe cause him for to die.
Immediately they led away Acetes out of sight,
And put him into prison strong from which there was no flight.
But while the cruell instruments of death as sword and fire
Were in preparing wherewithall t'accomplish Pentheys yre,
It is reported that the doores did of their owne accorde
Burst open and his chaines fall off. And yet this cruell Lorde
Persisteth fiercer than before, not bidding others go
But goes himselfe unto the hill Cytheron, which as tho
To Bacchus being consecrate did ring of chaunted songs,
And other loud confused sounds of Bacchus drunken throngs.
And even as when the bloudie Trumpe doth to the battell sound,
The lustie horse streight neying out bestirres him on the ground,
And taketh courage thereupon t'assaile his emnie proud:
Even so when Penthey heard afarre the noyse and howling loud
That Bacchus franticke folke did make, it set his heart on fire,
And kindled fiercer than before the sparks of settled ire.
There is a goodly plaine about the middle of the hill,
Environd in with Woods, where men may view eche way at will.
Here looking on these holie rites with lewde prophaned eyes
King Pentheys mother first of all hir foresaid sonne espies,
And like a Bedlem first of all she doth upon him runne,
And with hir Javeling furiously she first doth wound hir sonne.
Come hither sisters come, she cries, here is that mighty Bore,
Here is the Bore that stroyes our fieldes, him will I strike therefore.
With that they fall upon him all as though they had bene mad,
And clustring all upon a heape fast after him they gad.
He quakes and shakes: his words are now become more meeke and colde:
He now condemnes his owne default, and sayes he was too bolde.
And wounded as he was he cries: Helpe, Aunt Autonoe,
Now for Acteons blessed soule some mercie show to me.
She wist not who Acteon was, but rent without delay
His right hand off: and Ino tare his tother hand away.
To lift unto his mother tho the wretch had nere an arme:
But shewing hir his maimed corse, and woundes yet bleeding warme,
O mother see, he sayes: with that Agaue howleth out:
And writhed with hir necke awrie, and shooke hir haire about.
And holding from his bodie tome his head in bloudie hands,
She cries: fellowes in this deede our noble conquest stands.
No sooner could the winde have blowen the rotten leaves from trees,
When Winters frost hath bitten them, then did the hands of these
Most wicked women Pentheys limmes from one another teare.
The Thebanes being now by this example brought in feare,
Frequent this newfound sacrifice, and with sweete frankinsence
God Bacchus Altars lode with gifts in every place doe cense.

4.1:
Yet would not stout Alcithoe, Duke Mineus daughter, bow
Within the towne (of whose huge walles so monstrous high and thicke
This tale thus tolde a little space of pawsing was betwist,
She made an ende: and at hir tale all wondred: some denide
The Gods were pliant to hir boone. The bodies of them twaine
Then Bacchus name was reverenced through all the Theban coast,
Anon upon the same
Nought knoweth Cadmus that his daughter and hir little childe
But yet a comfort to them both in this their altred hew
Like as a Gally with hir nose doth cut the waters wide,
4.2:
The Orgies of this newfound God in conscience to allow
The fame is given Semyramis for making them of bricke)
And then began Leucothoe thus, hir sisters being whist:
Hir saying to be possible: and other some replide
Were mixt and joyned both in one. To both them did remaine
And Ino of hir Nephewes powre made every where great boast.
The furious Fiende Tisiphone doth cloth hir out of hand
Admitted were among the Goddes that rule the surges wilde.
Became that noble impe of theirs that Indie did subdew,
Enforced by the sweating armes of Rowers wyth the tide
4.3:
But still she stiffly doth denie that Bacchus is the sonne
Dwelt hard together two yong folke in houses joynde so nere
This Sunne that with his streaming light al worldly things doth cheare
That such as are in deede true Gods may all things worke at will:
One countnance: like as if a man should in one barke beholde
Of Cadmus daughters she alone no sorowes tasted had,
In garment streaming gorie bloud, and taketh in hir hand
Compellde with griefe and great mishappes that had ensewd togither,
Whom al Achaia worshipped with temples builded new.
Even so the monster with his brest did beare the waves aside,
4.4:
Of Jove: and in this heresie hir sisters with hir runne.
That under all one roofe well nie both twaine conveyed were.
Was tane in love. Of Phebus loves now list and you shall heare.
But Bacchus is not any such. Thys arguing once made still,
Two twigges both growing into one and still togither holde.
Save only that hir sisters haps perchaunce had made hir sad.
A burning Cresset steepte in bloud, and girdeth hir about
And straunge foretokens often seene since first his comming thither,
All only Acrise, Abas sonne, (though of the selfesame stocke)
And was now come as neere the rocke as well a man myght fling
4.5:
The Priest had bidden holiday, and that as well the Maide
The name of him was Pyramus, and Thisbe calde was she.
It is reported that this God did first of all espie,
To tell hir tale as others had Alcithoes turne was come.
Even so when through hir hugging and hir grasping of the tother
Now Juno noting how she waxt both proud and full of scorne,
With wreathed Snakes and so goes forth. And at hir going out,
He utterly forsakes his towne the which he builded had,
Remaind, who out of Argos walles unkindly did him locke,
Amid the pure and vacant aire a pellet from a sling.
4.6:
As Mistresse (for the time aside all other businesse layde)
So faire a man in all the East was none alive as he,
(For everie thing in Heaven and Earth is open to his eie)
Who with hir shettle shooting through hir web within the Loome,
The members of them mingled were and fastned both togither,
As well by reason of the sonnes and daughters she had borne,
Feare, terror, grief and pensivenesse for companie she tooke,
As though the fortune of the place so hardly him bestad,
And moved wilfull warre against his Godhead: thinking that
When on the sodaine Persey pusht his foote against the ground,
4.7:
In Buckskin cotes, with tresses loose, and garlondes on their heare,
Nor nere a woman, maide nor wife in beautie like to hir.
How Venus with the warlike Mars advoutrie did commit.
Said: Of the shepeheird Daphnyes love of Ida whom erewhile
They were not any lenger two: but (as it were) a toy
As also that she was advaunst by mariage in that towne
And also madnesse with his flaight, and gastly staring looke.
And not his owne. And fleeting long like pilgrims, at the last
There was not any race of Goddes, for he beleved not
And stied upward to the clouds his shadow did rebound
4.8:
Should in their hands the leavie speares (surnamed Thyrsis) beare,
This neighbrod bred acquaintance first, this neyghbrod first did stirre
It grieved him to see the fact and so discovered it,
A jealouse Nymph (bicause he did with Lemans hir beguile)
Of double shape. Ye could not say it was a perfect boy
To Athamas, King Aeolus sonne, a Prince of great renowne,
Within the house of Athamas no sooner foote she set,
Upon the coast of Illirie his wife and he were cast.
That Persey was the sonne of Jove: or that he was conceyved
Upon the sea: the beast ran fierce upon the passing shade.
4.9:
Foretelling them that if they did the Goddes commaundement breake,
The secret sparkes, this neighbrod first an entrance in did showe,
He shewed hir husband Junos sonne th'advoutrie and the place
For anger turned to a stone (such furie love doth sende: )
Nor perfect wench: it seemed both and none of both to beene.
But chiefly that hir sisters sonne who nourced was by hir
But that the postes began to quake and doores looke blacke as Jet.
Where ny forpind with cares and yeares, while of the chaunces past
By Danae of golden shower through which shee was deceived.
And as an Egle when he sees a Dragon in a glade
4.10:
He would with sore and grievous plagues his wrath upon them wreake.
For love to come to that to which it afterward did growe.
In which this privie scape was done. Who was in such a case
I will not speake: it is to knowe: ne yet I doe entende
Now when Hermaphroditus saw how in the water sheene
Was then exalted for a God: began thereat to stir,
The sonne withdrew him, Athamas and eke his wife were cast
Upon their house, and of their toyles and former travails tane
But yet ere long (such present force hath truth) he doth repent
Lie beaking of his blewish backe against the sunnie rayes,
4.11:
The women straight both yong and olde doe thereunto obay.
And if that right had taken place they had bene man and wife,
That heart and hand and all did faile in working for a space.
To tell how Scython variably digressing from his kinde,
To which he entred in a man, his limmes were weakened so
And freating at it in hirselfe said: Coulde this harlots burd
With ougly sightes in such a feare, that out of doores agast
They sadly talkt betweene themselves: Was my speare head the bane
As well his great impietie against God Bacchus meant,
Doth seize upon him unbeware, and with his talants layes
4.12:
Their yarne, their baskets, and their flax unsponne aside they lay,
But still their Parents went about to let which (for their life)
Anon he featly forgde a net of Wire so fine and slight,
Was sometime woman, sometime man, as liked best his minde.
That out fro thence but halfe a man he was compelde to go,
Transforme the Lydian watermen, and drowne them in the foord?
They would have fled. There stoode the Fiend, and stopt their passage out,
Of that same ougly Snake of Mars (quoth Cadmus) when I fled
As also that he did disdaine his Nephew for to knowe.
Sure holde upon his scalie necke lest writhing back his head
4.13:
And burne to Bacchus frankinsence. Whome solemly they call
They could not let. For both their heartes with equall flame did burne.
That neyther knot nor nooze therein apparant was to sight.
And Celmus also wyll I passe, who for bicause he cloong
He lifteth up his hands and said (but not with manly reere):
And make the mother teare the guttes in pieces of hir sonne?
And splaying forth hir filthie armes beknit with Snakes about,
From Sidon? or did I his teeth in ploughed pasture spred?
But Bacchus now full gloriously himselfe in Heaven doth showe.
His cruell teeth might doe him harme: so Persey in that stead
4.14:
By all the names and titles high that may to him befall:
No man was privie to their thoughts. And for to serve their turne
This piece of worke was much more fine than any handwarpe oofe
Most faithfully to Jupiter when Jupiter was yoong,
O noble father Mercurie, and Venus mother deere,
And Mineus al three daughters clad with wings, bicause they sponne

10.133: When Myrrha heard her father naamd, a greevous sygh she fet

10.135: Misdeemd not any wickednesse. But nerethelesse shee gest
10.136: There was some love: and standing in one purpose made request
10.137: To breake her mynd unto her, and shee set her tenderly
10.138: Uppon her lappe. The Ladye wept and sobbed bitterly.
10.139: Then culling her in feeble armes, shee sayd: I well espye
10.140: Thou art in love. My diligence in this behalf I sweare
10.141: Shall servisable to thee bee. Thou shalt not neede to feare
10.142: That ere thy father shall it knowe. At that same woord shee lept
10.143: From nurces lappe like one that had beene past her witts, and stept
10.144: With fury to her bed. At which shee leaning downe hir face
10.145: Sayd: Hence I pray thee: force mee not to shewe my shamefull cace.
10.146: And when the nurce did urge her still, shee answered eyther: Get
10.147: Thee hence, or ceace to aske mee why myself I thus doo fret.
10.148: The thing that thou desyrste to knowe is wickednesse. The old
10.149: Poore nurce gan quake, and trembling both for age and feare did hold
10.150: Her handes to her. And kneeling downe right humbly at her feete,
10.151: One whyle shee fayre intreated her with gentle woordes and sweete.
10.152: Another whyle (onlesse shee made her privie of her sorrow)
10.153: Shee threatned her, and put her in a feare shee would next morrow
10.154: Bewray her how shee went about to hang herself. But if
10.155: Shee told her, shee did plyght her fayth and help to her releef.
10.156: Shee lifted up her head, and then with teares fast gushing out
10.157: Beesloobered all her nurces brest: and going oft about
10.158: To speake, shee often stayd: and with her garments hid her face
10.159: For shame, and lastly sayd: O happye is my moothers cace
10.160: That such a husband hath. With that a greevous sygh shee gave,
10.161: And hilld her peace. Theis woordes of hers a trembling chilnesse drave
10.162: In nurcis limbes, which perst her bones: (for now shee understood
10.163: The cace) and all her horye heare up stiffly staring stood
10.164: And many things she talkt to put away her cursed love,
10.165: If that it had beene possible the madnesse to remove.
10.166: The Mayd herself to be full trew the councell dooth espye:
10.167: Yit if shee may not have her love shee fully myndes to dye.
10.168: Live still (quoth nurce) thou shalt obteine (shee durst not say thy father,
10.169: But stayd at that). And forbycause that Myrrha should the rather
10.170: Beleeve her, shee confirmd her woordes by othe. The yeerely feast
10.171: Of gentle Ceres came, in which the wyves bothe moste and least
10.172: Appareld all in whyght are woont the firstlings of the feeld,
10.173: Fyne garlonds made of eares of come, to Ceres for to yeeld.
10.174: And for the space of thryce three nyghts they counted it a sin
10.175: To have the use of any man, or once to towche his skin.
10.176: Among theis women did the Queene freequent the secret rites.
10.177: Now whyle that of his lawfull wyfe his bed was voyd a nightes,
10.178: The nurce was dooble diligent: and fynding Cinyras
10.179: Well washt with wyne, shee did surmyse there was a pretye lasse
10.180: In love with him. And hyghly shee her beawty setteth out.
10.181: And beeing asked of her yeeres, she sayd shee was about
10.182: The age of Myrrha. Well (quoth he) then bring her to my bed.
10.183: Returning home she sayd: bee glad my nurcechilde: we have sped.
10.184: Not all so wholly in her hart was wretched Myrrha glad,
10.185: But that her fore misgiving mynd did also make her sad.
10.186: Howbee't shee also did rejoyce as in a certaine kynd,
10.187: Such discord of affections was within her combred mynd.
10.188: It was the tyme that all things rest. And now Bootes bryght,
10.189: The driver of the Oxen seven, about the northpole pyght
10.190: Had sumwhat turnd his wayne asyde, when wicked Myrrha sped
10.191: About her buysnesse. Out of heaven the golden Phoebee fled.
10.192: With clowds more black than any pitch the starres did hyde their hed.
10.193: The nyght beecommeth utter voyd of all her woonted lyght.
10.194: And first before all other hid their faces out of syght
10.195: Good Icar and Erigonee, his daughter, who for love
10.196: Most vertuous to her fatherward, was taken up above
10.197: And made a starre in heaven. Three tymes had Myrrha warning given
10.198: By stumbling, to retyre. Three tymes the deathfull Owle that eeven
10.199: With doolefull noyse prognosticates unhappie lucke. Yet came
10.200: Shee forward still: the darknesse of the nyght abated shame.
10.201: Her left hand held her nurce, her right the darke blynd way did grope.
10.202: Anon shee to the chamber came: anon the doore was ope:
10.203: Anon she entred in. With that her foltring hammes did quake:
10.204: Her colour dyde: her blood and hart did cleerly her forsake.
10.205: The neerer shee approched to her wickednesse, the more
10.206: She trembled: of her enterpryse it irked her full sore:
10.207: And fayne shee would shee might unknowen have turned back. Nurce led
10.208: Her pawsing forward by the hand: and putting her to bed,
10.209: Heere, take this Damzell, Cinyras, shee is thine owne, shee sed.
10.210: And so shee layd them brest to brest. The wicked father takes
10.211: His bowelles into filthy bed, and there with wordes asslakes
10.212: The maydens feare, and cheeres her up. And lest this cryme of theyres
10.213: Myght want the ryghtfull termes, by chaunce as in respect of yeeres
10.214: He daughter did hir call, and shee him father. Beeing sped
10.215: With cursed seede in wicked womb, shee left her fathers bed,
10.216: Of which soone after shee became greate bagged with her shame.
10.217: Next night the lewdnesse doubled. And no end was of the same,
10.218: Untill at length that Cinyras desyrous for to knowe
10.219: His lover that so many nyghts uppon him did bestowe,
10.221: And eeke his daughter. Nathelesse, his sorrow at that time
10.222: Represt his speeche. Then hanging by he drew a Rapier bryght.
10.223: Away ran Myrrha, and by meanes of darknesse of the nyght
10.224: Shee was delivered from the death: and straying in the broade
10.225: Datebearing feeldes of Arabye, shee through Panchaya yode,
10.226: And wandring full nyne moonethes at length shee rested beeing tyrde
10.227: In Saba land. And when the tyme was neere at hand expyrde,
10.228: And that uneath the burthen of her womb shee well could beare,
10.229: Not knowing what she might desyre, distrest betweene the feare
10.230: Of death, and tediousnesse of lyfe, this prayer shee did make:
10.231: O Goddes, if of repentant folk you any mercye take,
10.232: Sharpe vengeance I confesse I have deserved, and content
10.233: I am to take it paciently. How bee it to th'entent
10.234: That neyther with my lyfe the quick, nor with my death the dead
10.235: Anoyed bee, from both of them exempt mee this same sted,
10.236: And altring mee, deny to mee both lyfe and death. We see
10.237: To such as doo confesse theyr faults sum mercy shewd to bee.
10.238: The Goddes did graunt her this request, the last that she should make.
10.239: The ground did overgrow hir feete, and ancles as she spake.
10.240: And from her bursten toes went rootes, which wrything heere and there
10.241: Did fasten so the trunk within the ground shee could not steare.
10.242: Her bones did into timber turne, whereof the marie was
10.243: The pith, and into watrish sappe the blood of her did passe.
10.244: Her armes were turnd to greater boughes, her fingars into twig,
10.245: Her skin was hardned into bark. And now her belly big
10.246: The eatching tree had overgrowen, and overtane her brest,
10.247: And hasted for to win her neck, and hyde it with the rest.
10.248: Shee made no taryence nor delay, but met the comming tree,
10.249: And shroonk her face within the barke therof. Although that shee
10.250: Togither with her former shape her senses all did loose,
10.251: Yit weepeth shee, and from her tree warme droppes doo softly woose.
10.252: The which her teares are had in pryce and honour. And the Myrrhe
10.253: That issueth from her gummy bark dooth beare the name of her,
10.254: And shall doo whyle the world dooth last. The misbegotten chyld
10.255: Grew still within the tree, and from his mothers womb defyld
10.256: Sought meanes to bee delyvered. Her burthende womb did swell
10.257: Amid the tree, and stretcht her out. But woordes wherwith to tell
10.258: And utter foorth her greef did want. She had no use of speech
10.259: With which Lucina in her throwes shee might of help beseech.
10.260: Yit like a woman labring was the tree, and bowwing downe
10.261: Gave often sighes, and shed foorth teares as though shee there should drowne.
10.262: Lucina to this wofull tree came gently downe, and layd
10.263: Her hand theron, and speaking woordes of ease the midwife playd.
10.264: The tree did cranye, and the barke deviding made away,
10.265: And yeelded out the chyld alyve, which cryde and wayld streyght way.
10.266: The waternymphes uppon the soft sweete hearbes the chyld did lay,
10.267: And bathde him with his mothers teares. His face was such as spyght
10.268: Must needes have praysd. For such he was in all condicions right,
10.269: As are the naked Cupids that in tables picturde bee.
10.270: But to th'entent he may with them in every poynt agree,
10.271: Let eyther him bee furnisshed with wings and quiver light,
10.272: Or from the Cupids take theyr wings and bowes and arrowes quight.

This graunt of his made Venus glad. Shee thankt him for the same.
And glyding through the aire uppon her yoked doves, shee came

Shee bade this river wash away what ever mortall were
In good Aenaeas bodye, and them under sea to beare.
The horned brooke fulfilld her hest, and with his water sheere

The better porcion of him did remayne unto him sownd.
His moother having hallowed him did noynt his bodye rownd

Endevering with theyr temples and theyr altars him to please.
Ascanius with the dowble name from thence began to reigne,
In whom the rule of Alba and of Latium did remayne.

And that the Grecians victorie becommes the Trojans weale.
But lest forgetting quyght themselves our horses happe to steale
Beyond the mark: the heaven and all that under heaven is found,
Dooth alter shape. So dooth the ground and all that is in ground.
And wee that of the world are part (considring how wee bee
Not only flesh, but also sowles, which may with passage free
Remove them into every kynd of beast both tame and wyld)
Let live in saufty honestly with slaughter undefyld,
The bodyes which perchaunce may have the spirits of our brothers,
Our sisters, or our parents, or the spirits of sum others
Alyed to us eyther by sum freendshippe or sum kin,
Or at the least the soules of men abyding them within.
And let us not Thyesteslyke thus furnish up our boordes
With bloodye bowells. Oh how leawd example he afoordes.
How wickedly prepareth he himself to murther man
That with a cruell knyfe dooth cut the throte of Calf, and can
Unmovably give heering to the lowing of the dam
Or sticke the kid that wayleth lyke the little babe, or eate
The fowle that he himself before had often fed with meate.
What wants of utter wickednesse in woorking such a feate?
What may he after passe to doo? well eyther let your steeres
Weare out themselves with woork, or else impute theyr death to yeeres.
Ageinst the wynd and weather cold let Wethers yeeld yee cotes,
And udders full of batling milk receyve yee of the Goates.
Away with sprindges, snares, and grinnes, away with Risp and net.
Away with guylefull feates: for fowles no lymetwiggs see yee set.
No feared fethers pitche yee up to keepe the Red deere in,
Ne with deceytfull bayted hooke seeke fishes for to win.
If awght doo harme, destroy it, but destroy't and doo no more.
Forbeare the flesh: and feede your mouthes with fitter foode therfore.
15.132: Even so to Agamemnons great renowne gives Atreus place,
15.133: Even so Achilles deedes, the deedes of Peleus doo abace.
15.134: Even so beyond Aegaeus, farre dooth Theseyes prowesse go.
15.135: And (that I may examples use full matching theis) even so
15.136: Is Saturne lesse in fame than Jove. Jove rules the heavenly spheres,
15.137: And all the tryple shaped world. And our Augustus beares
15.138: Dominion over all the earth. They bothe are fathers: they
15.139: Are rulers both. Yee Goddes to whom both fyre and swoord gave way,
15.140: What tyme yee with Aenaeas came from Troy: yee Goddes that were
15.141: Of mortall men canonyzed: thou Quirin whoo didst reere
15.142: The walles of Rome: and Mars who wart the valeant Quirins syre
15.143: And Vesta of the household Goddes of Caesar with thy fyre
15.144: Most holy: and thou Phebus whoo with Vesta also art
15.145: Of household: and thou Jupiter whoo in the hyghest part
15.146: Of mountayne Tarpey hast thy Church: and all yee Goddes that may
15.147: With conscience sauf by Poets bee appealed to: I pray
15.148: Let that same day bee slowe to comme and after I am dead,
15.149: In which Augustus (whoo as now of all the world is head)
15.150: Quyght giving up the care therof ascend to heaven for ay,
15.151: There (absent hence) to favour such as unto him shall pray.
15.152: Now have I brought a woork to end which neither Joves feerce wrath,
15.153: Nor swoord, nor fyre, nor freating age with all the force it hath
15.154: Are able to abolish quyght. Let comme that fatall howre
15.155: Which (saving of this brittle flesh) hath over mee no powre,
15.156: And at his pleasure make an end of myne uncerteyne tyme.
15.157: Yit shall the better part of mee assured bee to clyme
15.158: Aloft above the starry skye. And all the world shall never
15.159: Be able for to quench my name. For looke how farre so ever
15.160: The Romane Empyre by the ryght of conquest shall extend,
15.161: So farre shall all folke reade this woork. And tyme without all end
15.162: (If Poets as by prophesie about the truth may ame)
15.163: My lyfe shall everlastingly bee lengthened still by fame.
